speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-RESPONSIBILITY FOR DECISION NOT TO INFORM INTERMEDIARIES OF COUNTRY OFFERING TO RECEIVE INMATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Prime Minister concerning the tragic events at the British Columbia Penitentiary. Who made the decision not to provide the information of the offer from an unidentified

June 12, 1975
Oral Questions
country to the intermediaries between the inmates and hostages on the one hand and the authorities on the other? These intermediaries were again to meet those in the vault some three hours after the information concerning the offer from an unidentified country had initially been received by the Prime Minister.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-RESPONSIBILITY FOR DECISION NOT TO INFORM INTERMEDIARIES OF COUNTRY OFFERING TO RECEIVE INMATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not quite sure at what level the communication had been communicated downwards. I was not responsible for that, but I think the responsibility for deciding who would be told is within the Solicitor General's authority. I would be prepared to say that I made the decision that we should not just tell the criminals that another country had offered to receive them until we had worked out a lot of other details.

subsubtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-RESPONSIBILITY FOR DECISION NOT TO INFORM INTERMEDIARIES OF COUNTRY OFFERING TO RECEIVE INMATES
speechtext: The Prime Minister said he made the offer to tell the inmates that?

subsubtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-RESPONSIBILITY FOR DECISION NOT TO INFORM INTERMEDIARIES OF COUNTRY OFFERING TO RECEIVE INMATES
speechtext: No. I said I would be as responsible as anyone for having made the decision not to tell the inmates that a country was prepared to receive them until certain consultations had taken place in British Columbia and until certain contingencies had been prepared for.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-REASON INTERMEDIARIES NOT ASKED FOR PROBABLE REACTION OF INMATES TO OFFER OF COUNTRY TO RECEIVE THEM

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-REASON INTERMEDIARIES NOT ASKED FOR PROBABLE REACTION OF INMATES TO OFFER OF COUNTRY TO RECEIVE THEM
speechtext: should like to ask the Prime Minister whether arrangements were made for consultation as the Prime Minister had indicated, and, if this was to be a matter for further study and consideration with the decision being ultimately made by members of the government here as to what was to happen next day, why was there not an earlier request by the Prime Minister and the Solicitor General to have an early assessment from the negotiators who were, I understand, the only ones who were in contact with the inmates and the prisoners, as to what would be their probable reaction to such a proposal, such an offer from this unidentified country? Why was there not a proper request for consultation with the intermediaries and feedback of their views to the Prime Minister, the Solicitor General and others? I ask this question particularly in view of the fact that everybody had been in this cell for 40 hours, obviously under conditions which might lead to a blow-up of some sort.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-REASON INTERMEDIARIES NOT ASKED FOR PROBABLE REACTION OF INMATES TO OFFER OF COUNTRY TO RECEIVE THEM
speechtext: I am endeavouring to understand the question and the suggestion. Is it that we should have hypothetically asked the inmates what they would do if some country was prepared to receive them?

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-REASON INTERMEDIARIES NOT ASKED FOR PROBABLE REACTION OF INMATES TO OFFER OF COUNTRY TO RECEIVE THEM
speechtext: My question was this: why did the Prime Minister and the Solicitor General not request an immediate expression of opinion from the intermediaries as to how the inmates would react to the knowledge of such a proposal?

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-REASON INTERMEDIARIES NOT ASKED FOR PROBABLE REACTION OF INMATES TO OFFER OF COUNTRY TO RECEIVE THEM
speechtext: Then the suggestion is, I take it, that before the knowledge that some country might accept them-how could we ask them what their reaction would be to certain information which never existed?

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-REASON INTERMEDIARIES NOT ASKED FOR PROBABLE REACTION OF INMATES TO OFFER OF COUNTRY TO RECEIVE THEM
speechtext: May I remind the right hon. gentleman that according to public information, the Prime Minister and the Solicitor General had this knowledge some three hours before the intermediaries were going to see the inmates again that evening. Is the Prime Minister suggesting-I do not want to be argumentative, Mr. Speaker- that there was no time under these conditions to get an opinion from the intermediaries as to how the inmates would react to the knowledge of that offer? Was there no time for the government to get that information before everything was sort of shut down for the night?

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-REASON INTERMEDIARIES NOT ASKED FOR PROBABLE REACTION OF INMATES TO OFFER OF COUNTRY TO RECEIVE THEM
speechtext: Things were not shut down for the night. The Solicitor General and his officials and, indeed, ministers, were involved in this situation from the outset. We were examining various hypotheses which might fulfil themselves; we were working on various contingency plans. I told the House yesterday, and so did the Solicitor General, that as soon as we had some kind of positive answer from a country we began discussing the way in which it could best be put to the inmates, and the time at which it could best be put to them. I think the House and the country must understand that it would not necessarily have been a good solution for us to have bundled up both the criminals and the hostages and sent them off to a certain country. It is obvious that we had in some way to separate the hostages from the criminals, and it was a matter of finding a way in which this could best be done.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-PERSONS CONSULTED ON OFFER OF COUNTRY TO RECEIVE PRISONERS-POSSIBLE CONSULTATION WITH INTERMEDIARIES

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-PERSONS CONSULTED ON OFFER OF COUNTRY TO RECEIVE PRISONERS-POSSIBLE CONSULTATION WITH INTERMEDIARIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Prime Minister. Yesterday in Hansard, as reported at page 6644, the Prime Minister said that with regard to the consideration of the offer by a foreign government the government was determining policy but "as the Solicitor General indicated in his answer, in consultation with the people who were in contact with the criminals". Since the intermediaries, from what we can gather, apparently knew nothing before their last visit to the vault, just who among the people in contact with the criminals were consulted in fact?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-PERSONS CONSULTED ON OFFER OF COUNTRY TO RECEIVE PRISONERS-POSSIBLE CONSULTATION WITH INTERMEDIARIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I could not give names even if I had them, but that is what I had in mind in my first answer this afternoon when I said that I did not know at what level consultations with the people on the spot had taken place. After I spoke to the Solicitor General some time after eleven o'clock the night before last, he was to talk to his people on the spot to proceed with our plan to have certain consultations. I do not know exactly at what level those consultations were.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-PERSONS CONSULTED ON OFFER OF COUNTRY TO RECEIVE PRISONERS-POSSIBLE CONSULTATION WITH INTERMEDIARIES
speechtext:
Then it is regrettable, Mr. Speaker, that the Solicitor General is not here today. In his absence perhaps the Prime Minister could answer
June 12, 1975

this question. Did the Prime Minister ask the Solicitor General to discuss this new situation with the intermediaries, and was the Prime Minister told by someone that these intermediaries were in fact being consulted on what should be done and, if so, who told the Prime Minister that these consultations were taking place?

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-PERSONS CONSULTED ON OFFER OF COUNTRY TO RECEIVE PRISONERS-POSSIBLE CONSULTATION WITH INTERMEDIARIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I did not direct the Solicitor General to speak to the intermediaries necessarily, those who were in contact with the inmates. I told him that he should get the people on the spot who were under his authority to report to him on the situation, and then to contact me and we would make other decisions.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-GOVERNMENT VIEW OF ACCEPTABILITY OF OFFER OF COUNTRY TO RECEIVE PRISONERS

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-GOVERNMENT VIEW OF ACCEPTABILITY OF OFFER OF COUNTRY TO RECEIVE PRISONERS
speechtext: A final supplementary question, Mr. Speaker, Yesterday, as reported at page 6643 of Hansard, the Prime Minister said that the second priority was to make sure "that the criminals themselves did not escape into some other country where they would go unharmed, and this was a priority that the government was determined to follow". At any time during the five hours preceding the resolution of this tragic event at the penitentiary did the government make up its mind that the offer of the unnamed country was acceptable in principle and, if so, when was that decision made and what was it?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-GOVERNMENT VIEW OF ACCEPTABILITY OF OFFER OF COUNTRY TO RECEIVE PRISONERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, no, it would be impossible to make up one's mind in principle. It was important in the absolute present circumstances, not in theory but in practice, to know in which way we would separate the hostages from the criminals and that is what we were working at. I must remind the hon. member that if we had wanted to wash our hands of this it would have been relatively simple to bundle up the criminals and the hostages, put them on a plane and send them to some other country. But we felt it was better to take our responsibilities in Canada and to trust our guards and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to take whatever action was necessary to ensure that separation, rather than to send Canadian hostages whom we wanted to hold harmless into some other country.

Oral Questions
wound, may I ask the Prime Minister this. In view of the fact that the government, as of necessity, has to be so intimately involved in this problem and in the decision making process, will the Prime Minister now reconsider yesterday's decision, announced by the Solicitor General, that it was preparing an inquiry under the Penitentiaries Act, which limits the inquiry to only a departmental investigation and not a public inquiry? Would he now reconsider that decision and call for a full public inquiry under the Inquiries Act so that someone outside the penitentiaries system can come in and assess this entire situation, which of necessity would include the decision made at that time by both those on the scene and those away from the scene?

I had not
received any directly, Mr. Speaker, but in my communications with the Solicitor General it was indicated that the state of play was still as I indicated earlier, that consultations were going on, they were being assessed and plans were being made before the unfortunate series of events took place which brought the whole matter to a close.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my last question concerns the new evidence that those who were involved in the mediation are concerned about, that is being excluded from the discussions toward the end of this unfortunate incident. Can the Prime Minister advise why the negotiators were suddenly excluded from the negotiations toward the end of that evening, I understand it was around eleven o'clock, and why no further negotiations or discussions took place between the mediators and the officials on the site? Why was it that these

Oral Questions
mediators were asked to leave, or why they went home? As a corollary to that question, I would urge the Prime Minister to again consider the matter of a public inquiry in view of the many, many questions which are now arising in the public mind. I would appreciate a response in terms of why the mediators were excluded toward the end of that evening.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-REASON FOR EXCLUSION OF INTERMEDIARIES FROM NEGOTIATIONS BEFORE CONCLUSION OF INCIDENT INVOLVING PRISONERS AND HOSTAGES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not know to what series of facts the hon. member is referring. I do not know what meetings they were excluded from and I do not know why. I am sure that when the Solicitor General is in full command of the facts he will make them known to the House, and I think this can be done without any type of inquiry. He will get to the bottom of the facts by himself. If he cannot do it that way he will, as he indicated yesterday, appoint an inquiry. The rest is a matter of policy and political judgment. I repeat that the minister, the government and myself are prepared to take the responsibility for the handling of these events. I must point out to the House that I did consult with the leaders of the three opposition parties on this matter, asking if they had any advice to give me. We had a good, frank exchange on a confidential basis. Then, the government went out and took its responsibilities. I repeat, the political and policy decisions were ours. There is no need for an inquiry to find out what they are; we are telling you what they are.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-REASON FOR EXCLUSION OF INTERMEDIARIES FROM NEGOTIATIONS BEFORE CONCLUSION OF INCIDENT INVOLVING PRISONERS AND HOSTAGES
speechtext: I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I just want to make it clear, and I know the Prime Minister did not want to give any other impression, that the consultations took place long before this offer from an unidentified country had been received by the government.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-REASON FOR EXCLUSION OF INTERMEDIARIES FROM NEGOTIATIONS BEFORE CONCLUSION OF INCIDENT INVOLVING PRISONERS AND HOSTAGES
speechtext: That is quite right, Mr. Speaker. I did not intend to indicate that the responsibility was other than ours. Obviously, we did not get together after eleven o'clock that evening. I am trying to make clear to the House that we have two fundamental objectives that we are trying to pursue. One, which I am sure will have the support of this House, is not to create a situation where people in other penitentiaries or indeed in the same penitentiary might think that if they took similar action they would get safe conduct and be set free. This will not happen under my government.

subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-REASON FOR EXCLUSION OF INTERMEDIARIES FROM NEGOTIATIONS BEFORE CONCLUSION OF INCIDENT INVOLVING PRISONERS AND HOSTAGES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext:
That the House deplores the action of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development in moving toward policies of a paternalistic and bureaucratic nature with respect to native people and specifically requests that a moratorium be placed on the implementation of recent guidelines issued by the department until such time as full consultation has taken place with the native people.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it may seem somewhat superfluous, but let me say in introducing this motion that I cannot overemphasize the seriousness and importance my colleagues and I attach to this debate. Although the major debate on the motion will be centred around the recently imposed guidelines, it is important to note-and I want to stress it-that this is a symptom of a more serious, chronic illness that has and continues to plague the native people of Canada.
We will be dealing with some very fundamental principles throughout this debate. With the introduction of new

June 12, 1975

policies under the guise of program circulars, the minister and the government are once again embarking upon a regressive course of action that in recent times can be compared with the 1969 white paper on Indian Affairs. At the outset, I want to say to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Buchanan), for whom I have great respect, that he has not been completely informed as to the implications of many of the policies contained in the guidelines, and has failed to recognize the serious consequences and implications they will have not only on the future of the native people but in his future relationships with the native community. Without exception, the native leaders across Canada who have had an opportunity to study the guidelines have unequivocally rejected them and have called for a moratorium so that detailed analysis and response can be made by the native people. On the specific point of native awareness of the guidelines, I want to emphasize that the large number of Indian leaders with whom I have talked or communicated have little or no knowledge of the guidelines, let alone an opportunity to assess them in detail. As recently as one o'clock today I had a call from a very large Indian representation in Ontario that had little or no knowledge of these guidelines or time to assess them in detail.
This, in itself, is an extremely serious situation, one in which the minister and the Department of Indian Affairs are introducing new policies, extensive in content and detail, which are completely foreign to many of the native leaders. The native people have been subjected to similar tactics in the past and this situation in itself deserves a thorough investigation by the minister and an immediate withdrawal of the guidelines until such time as the investigation is completed.
In the past few weeks we have attempted to convince the minister that he is embarking upon a program which will impede native development in the attempt to gain self-sufficiency and rid themselves of paternalistic, bureaucratic control by government. Unfortunately, our expressed concerns have not been heeded. The proposals contained in the guidelines will ensure a continuation of the bondage of native people to the federal government and, what is more serious, will prevent them from growing and developing in a positive manner.
I want to emphasize the principal issue in this debate. Let there be no doubt in the minds of the minister and the government that the issue is full consultation with the native community to evolve over a period of time a format whereby the native people of Canada, through self-determination, can establish their own priorities administered by local government free from the yoke of bureaucracy.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext:
I emphasize this point because the minister, in responding to repeated questions, has attempted to divert the House, the native people and the people of Canada from this major issue by repeated references to accountability. Let me state as emphatically as I can that accountability is not the issue; accountability did not precipitate this debate. We accept the principle of accountability, and from my discussions with native leaders across
Indian Affairs
Canada I can say there has been universal acceptance on their part of the need for good accounting practices. Indeed, I am certain the minister knows that at the present time a majority of the bands in Canada have accounting procedures which are more than adequate. In fact, the native leaders told me it would have been more productive and of greater benefit to the native people if the minister had started with an internal self-cleansing of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
I am sure a number of my colleagues will enlarge on this theme during the debate, but I would like to take a few moments to place this specific question in perspective by quoting from a discussion paper entitled "Principles of Indian Government." This document, prepared by the Saskatchewan Federation of Indians to express their concern about the guidelines, forcefully defines the importance they attach to accountability-a concern which is shared by native people across Canada. It states:
The strengthening of the band accounting and reporting systems has been insisted upon by the chiefs and councils of this region. Contrary to the assumption of government, the Saskatchewan Indian bands are in unanimous agreement that accountability is of the utmost importance. They do wish to be accountable both to the funding source and to their own band membership.
As I observed a few moments ago, this view expressed by the Saskatchewan Federation of Indians is undoubtedly shared by the native leaders with whom I have had numerous consultations. What are some of the specific issues which would have such a destructive effect on the native people? In what manner has the minister eroded the trust and confidence which is so essential when dealing with the difficult and complex problems of native people? In the long-term view, this lack of trust and confidence may well be the most serious consequence of the government's present actions. Surely the minister realized the enormity of the native problems and the necessity of approaching them with understanding, patience and sensitivity on a foundation of mutual trust and confidence.
I should like to ask the minister this question: how long will it take him and the government to recognize they must have respect for the native community, for their leaders and their judgment, if they in turn are to hope for the same respect for their role as leaders in Ottawa? I should like the minister to reflect on that question.
The most serious breach of trust and confidence has been the absence of consultation with the native people. Despite the minister's assertions to the contrary, consultation has not taken place with native leaders; these guidelines, containing many new policies, have been introduced in a unilateral fashion. I want to remind the House that we are not talking about two or three pages of changes, but about an extensive series of alterations so mind-boggling in magnitude and so complex in content that experts in several fields will be required to fully understand their impact.
A cursory glance at these guidelines makes it perfectly clear that the end product was not conceived overnight. There can be no doubt that the time-frame extending from their embryonic stage of development to their final form has spanned a period far greater than the minister's time in office. Surely such a lengthy interval in the absence of

June 12, 1975
Indian Affairs
full consultation with the native leaders is clear evidence of the government's intention to introduce the measure in a unilateral manner.
The issue of consultation is critical because the absence of consultation clearly shows the government's intention to make unilateral policy changes. I can assure the House that if the native people had been privy to the details of the guidelines, and if they had been offered the opportunity to make an equal and substantive input toward their formulation, the principle of self-government would have been preserved and this debate today would have been unnecessary.
Let me briefly review the record. As recently as June 2 of this year, in response to repeated questioning on this side of the House a communique was issued by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development entitled "Information Summary of Local Government Guidelines for Band Councils and Innuit Settlements." We read on page 2:
The minister (the Hon. Judd Buchanan) repeated these assurances in the House of Commons on May 6,1975.
"We are prepared to regard these guidelines as being of an interim nature. If they create difficulties and problems, we are prepared to change them."
This communique was sent out on a national basis. Mr. Speaker, the statement I have just quoted is not only a misrepresentation of the exchange which took place between the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Die-fenbaker) and the minister, but it is a contradiction of the facts as I know them prior to and subsequent to that exchange in the House of Commons. I believe it is necessary to review that exchange between my right hon. friend and the minister if we are to understand the significance of that statement. I should like to quote the following from Hansard of May 6, 1975, at page 5509:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question directed to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has to do with the policy circulars which have been issued by his department concerning Indian rights and obligations. As the Federation of Saskatchewan Indians as well as the chiefs of the various tribes in that province have taken strong objection to those circulars, on the ground that they were drafted without Indian consultation and represent an arbitrary, bureaucratic action, and that the implementation of the guidelines would result in the loss of their tribal identity, would the minister be prepared to hold back the application of these guidelines and circulars until there has been the fullest consultation, so that the Queen's wards shall not have their rights sacrificed in any way?
The following is the minister's response:
Mr. Speaker, the right hon. member has, I take it, referred to the local government guidelines and the education guidelines. First, I do not accept the suggestion that there has not been consultation. There has been considerable consultation on these guidelines ... with the Indian people, or the National Indian Brotherhood. I indicated to them in a letter that the ones which have been proclaimed will remain in force, but we regard them as being of an interim nature and will review them at the end of the year. With respect to the ones which have not been proclaimed, we would wait for their response, which would be in addition to the discussions we have had to date and we shall give them until June 1 to respond to the ones which have not yet been put into force.
Two observations must be made and developed about the minister's response, which clearly indicates that unilateral action was in fact taken and that there has been an

absence of consultation. To paraphrase, the minister referred to "local government guidelines" and "education guidelines", known respectively to those who have studied the problem as series D and and series E. The minister also implied in his response that these guidelines had been proclaimed and that they will remain in force. This, of course, is precisely the point I am making and that my colleagues will be making, that indeed these guidelines have been proclaimed unilaterally and it is this action by the government that has been rejected by the native community.
On this particular point, I want to emphasize that the assistant deputy minister of Indian and Eskimo affairs, in correspondence with regional directors on February 17 of this year, clearly indicated that program circular D-l contained the general terms and conditions for all programs and in fact was the cornerstone of Indian local government policy. So in fact, contrary to what the minister would have us believe, the key guidelines have been introduced and are to remain in force. Again, on May 20 of this year, in response to questions put by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Malone), as reported at page 5950 of Hansard the minister replied:
These are guidelines which we have established for the operation of local government on the reserves. We feel they are reasonable guidelines having to do with normal administration, auditing and so on. We are asking the bands to agree to them and we expect they will be prepared to do so.
To a supplementary question regarding the guidelines, the minister responded as follows:
As far as these guidelines are concerned, I have already indicated to the Indian people that we are prepared to regard them as being of an interim nature. We would discuss them and review them after they have been in operation for a year. There are further guidelines which have not yet been proclaimed and we have stated we are prepared to hear any representations regarding them.
Then on May 26, in questions in the House respecting the guidelines, the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) specifically asked for an assurance that band funding would not be conditional upon the acceptance of local government guidelines. The minister, as reported at page 6097 of Hansard, replied as follows:
We have indicated that the guidelines which have been proclaimed will be going into force, but we are prepared, prior to the beginning of the next fiscal year, to discuss them and alter them if that seems the prudent course. We have indicated they are in effect. As to the other ones which have not yet been put in place, we are prepared to hear representations on them before they come into effect.
Again, Mr. Speaker, it is very clear that the important guidelines, specifically D-l and series E, are in effect and were planned to be put into effect with no consultation and by unilateral action. The assistant deputy minister of Indian and Eskimo affairs, in correspondence with regional directors on February 17 stated, if I may quote his letter to the regional director, Alberta region, headed "Local Government Program, General Terms and Conditions":
Attached is an updated version of the general terms and conditions sent to you in September, 1974. You will note that they have been put into program circular format and are now designated "Program Circular D-l" with the title: "General Terms and Conditions-Local Government Program". These general terms and conditions encompass all programs and are the cornerstone of Indian local government policy and contain the non-negotiable conditions as seen from the federal government's point of view. While suggestions for amendments or
June 12, 1975

improvements are solicited, these terms and conditions remain mandatory.
There can be no doubt, Mr. Speaker, from the minister's statements and from correspondence from the department that these guidelines were introduced in a unilateral manner, with the prospect of their remaining in force. What is even more serious, and in my view deserves the immediate attention of the minister, is the fear that these guidelines are being forced on the native people. Again I want to refer to the letter dated February 17 from the assistant deputy minister, the next succeeding paragraph. He writes:
Attached as well are copies of Program Circulars D-2 and D-3 which deal with district council operations and band core funding respectively. Program circulars D-4 and D-5 will follow, in due course, covering band program funding and band program administration funding.
Then later in that paragraph:
In the interim, you should delay the approval of any band council resolutions dealing with program administration funding for the coming fiscal year. In order that programs continue uninterrupted, you may advance funds to bands for the first quarter only based on this year's arrangements.
I do not pretend to be a lawyer or to understand that type of language, but in my view there can be no doubt that coercion is implied and I strongly urge the minister to investigate this particular problem; because if such were the case, then of course it would be an injustice of the gravest magnitude.
The second point in connection with the minister's responses on May 6 was his reference to consultation on these guidelines, and I think he referred either to the Indian people or the National Indian Brotherhood. Once again, the facts do not support the minister's position. As I indicated at the outset, there has been widespread rejection of the guidelines and the major complaint in each instance has been the absence of consultation. I should like to quote from a letter that was addressed to the minister on May 30 of this year by the National Indian Brotherhood. The first part of the letter reads as follows:
Enclosed you will find a paper which we have prepared for your attention. In your letter to me of April 21, 1975, and in more recent public statements, you express surprise that Indian organizations are opposing the guidelines issued by the Department of Indian Affairs. We believe that this paper will clarify our position and convince you of the justice of our opposition.
On the same subject, I am very concerned about another statement you have been making. It concerns the consultation which took place on the guidelines. To my knowledge there has been no consultation at any time between your Department and the National Indian Brotherhood on the five Local Government Program Circulars. In regard to the twelve Education Circulars, there are certain aspects that you did not emphasize.
The letter was signed by the president of the National Indian Brotherhood. Again, on January 2 of this year a press release was issued by the National Indian Brotherhood. The subject of the press release was "National Indian Brotherhood Protests Minister's Statement on 'Consultation' ".
I quote from this press release which states in part:
Contrary to several recent public statements made by the minister, Mr. Manuel denies that there has been any consultation between the brotherhood and the department on the five Local Government Guide-
Indian Affairs
lines. The consultation which took place on the Education Guidelines resulted in rejection by the Indian organization.
Mr. Manuel protests a process of consultation based on reaction to bureaucratically prepared blue-prints designed to govern the lives of Indian people.
I have received numerous examples from provincial organizations similar to this, from various bands, tribes and individuals, but they are far too lengthy to list in Hansard. They are well documented and are available for those who wish to see them on a subsequent occasion. As I indicated at the outset, these guidelines contain proposals which have serious implications and will unquestionably place the right of self-government by native people in jeopardy. I know my colleagues will discuss many of these aspects and specifics this afternoon. I also know, as I am sure the minister does, that these guidelines are so extensive that it would be impossible, in fact, in the length of time at our disposal to cover all the aspects involved affecting Indian rights.
I believe the fears of the native people can best be summarized by quoting from a letter to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), dated April 17 of this year, from the president of the National Indian Brotherhood following a special general assembly meeting held in Ottawa in March of this year. The letter states:
Following is a resolution passed by our special general assembly, held in Ottawa, Ontario, on March 25-27, 1975:
Motion: (Alec Kennedy, Max Gros-Louis)
That the executive council direct the cabinet to clearly tell the minister of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development that he should no longer implement the white paper policy of 1969 in any way, shape or form.
Carried.
In so far as the National Indian Brotherhood and the chiefs of Alberta met with you-
That was in June, 1970.
-and were assured by yourself personally that your government would not pursue the proposals outlined in the white paper policy of 1969; and further, in so far as your former minister of Indian affairs ... had assured us on numerous occasions that his department would not attempt to implement the concepts outlined in the 1969 white paper, we are very concerned to find that many aspects of this above-mentioned proposed policy are now evident in new program guidelines and regulations being imposed on our band councils.
These new program guidelines and regulations essentially represent changes in the department's policies and programs and impinge upon negotiations respecting Indian rights, currently under way.
Let me conclude very briefly by indicating that the guidelines as we have seen them from the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development are but another example of the continuing paternalistic attitude of the government. The formula of divide and conquer is well known to the native people, and this is but another example of the government's plan to control and manipulate the native people of Canada.
Contrary to what the minister would have us believe, this introduction of an unbelievable number of regulations-I would ask hon. members opposite to take the time to review these-will restrict local government and the ability of the native people to establish their own priorities and deal with problems which are specific to the needs of their people. I am sure that if hon. members reviewed all the aspects of these regulations and assessed them in

June 12, 1975
Indian Affairs
detail, they would not be willing to live under these guidelines whether they were native persons or not.
Perhaps we should not be surprised by this attitude, because it is an attitude that I have found permeates many aspects of governments. Each day we see infringement on an increasing number of our personal rights as the government and bureaucracy decides what is best for us as individuals. The native people reject bureaucratic control, and in the matter before the House I strongly oppose any measures that will adversely effect local autonomy of the native community. These guidelines are a total rejection of the right to local autonomy. We are not dealing with guidelines respecting the rights of the people; we are dealing with a bureaucratic, imposed government of the native people by way of regulation.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are not dealing with a new subject today. On several occasions you have heard me ramble on about policy guidelines, you have heard some of my colleagues to my right speaking about them, and you have heard a prepared statement on the matter read out in the House on behalf of the minister by someone else's parliamentary secretary. Even the minister himself has spoken on this subject.
Much of the time was spent discussing the meaning of the word "consultation". I do not wish to take up much more time of the House discussing that, but I would just like to point out that if one party to a decision says there was consultation, and the other party says there was not, then very obviously there has been a breakdown in communications somewhere. That is an important concept that often gets buried under a flurry of circulars, guidelines, press releases and excerpts from Hansard, tons of paper, but no communication!
By my definition, communication takes place when one person listens while another speaks; then you reverse that pattern, think about it for a while and repeat the whole process until a decision is reached. That is communication. The Department of Indian Affairs does not appear to use that method. It seems to me that their definition involves having top-level bureaucrats make the decision; then one of them writes it up as a speech which the minister reads; then they bring in a high-powered team of public relations people to make sure the official word is spread far and wide; then they get some lower-level bureaucrat to go out to the Indian communities to tell the Indian people how they will live for the next little while.
By using this method there is no provision for feedback from the native people. It seems to me the department has adopted the idea that Indians are not people, that they are non-people, just things to be administered. It is not for any lack of trying on behalf of the native people that this lack of communication exists. Some of the entities the department considers non-people try to communicate by forming organizations. There is a group of them about four blocks from where we are sitting today. I refer to the National Indian Brotherhood. They have an office on the sixteenth floor of a skyscraper. They have secretaries and legal counsel. Some of them even wear ties.

The existence of this particular type of non-person owes no thanks to the government. It is the taxpayers' money that is being spent, money that was earned by these people a long time ago. This particular type of non-person is pretty sophisticated. On the surface he would appear to be much like other middle-class Canadians. But he is trying to communicate with the department and is treated by the department like a non-person.
There are other non-people. There are people like myself who are elected to an august body such as this. We try to communicate our problems. We try to tell the other people in the country that native people do not have a share of the great Canadian pie. It is obvious that the department does not listen to us.
Then there are the other non-people who are trying to communicate. They are not as sophisticated as the members of the National Indian Brotherhood up in the skyscraper. They do not have as lavish a platform as the non-person who is speaking now. However, they are still trying to communicate. They show that the department treats them as nobodies by getting drunk occasionally on the streets, and sometimes by bleeding on the lawns of the House of Commons. Many members will recall the incidents that occurred here last fall.
We are attempting to communicate, but nobody listens to us. Proof of that fact is the situation we are discussing today. The native people want to say to the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development that they do not want to be treated any more like non-people. There are several ways in which one can be a somebody in Canada. One way is to spend a lot of money on mufflers: we see that advertisement on TV once in a while. The other is to have a voice in the decisions which affect one's life.
The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has proved, by its handling of the guidelines, that it is not willing to let the Indian people have a say in their own lives. The department will not treat us as somebodies. The department has proved that all the Indian people who try to communicate, can try to communicate until they are blue in the face but that the department, the minister and the top bureaucrats, will not listen.
I finally found the document to which the minister is more than likely to refer when he speaks about consultation. I refer to the report of the task force set up to review the grants to bands program. In the course of its one-year life, members of this task force talked to about 28 native groups and received submissions from another 13. They reported to the minister in April, 1973. If one reads the recommendations of this committee, one can see the seeds that eventually grew into the program policy guidelines circular. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, it would seem that some Indian people had a small part to play in planting those seeds.
However, the plant, the circular, grew under the loving care of the bureaucrats of the department. It grew from the seeds in 1973 until February, 1975, when it came out of the department's hothouse. The problem is that when this plant came out, the Indian people saw it for the first time in two years. At that time they could not recognize it. There had been no Indian hands pruning, fertilizing or

going around spraying the plant to eliminate the weeds, and so on.
Is it any wonder the Indian people across the country reject this plant, these circulars? Most provincial Indian organizations have flatly rejected these circulars. Those provincial organizations which have not rejected them are asking for more time in which to study and comment on the necessary changes. I have their comments here, if the minister would care to look at them. They may seem familiar to him because he has them already.
If the minister had taken time from his busy schedule to read a little and listen a little, he would realize how ugly this plant circular is to the eyes of Indians across this lovely land of ours. The hon. member who introduced the motion we are addressing ourselves to now has asked for a moratorium on the implementation of these circulars. That would be a good thing if it happened; but that would not be sufficient. As a matter of fact, I suggested that it should be tossed in the garbage.
In the short time the minister has occupied the Indian affairs portfolio he has ruined any possibility of ever communicating with the Indian people. Communication is a two-way exchange. The minister has proved time and time again that he will not listen. He has surrounded himself with administrators who seem to have adopted the motto "At Indian affairs you are a nobody." I am speaking of administrators such as Jim Wright and John McGilip. Jim Wright is now acting regional director in Saskatchewan. He is doing such a good job of communicating with the Indian people that they now refuse to attend meetings at which he is present. They even refuse to allow him into their communities. He is a good man to have around in a department charged with administering the affairs of Indian people!
Then there is Mr. John McGilip, a man with an impressive background. In fact, he is a model public servant. He received his training in the art of administering non-people in one of the finest schools in the world, the British colonial civil service. The Indian people do not trust him. They do not even trust him to be a messenger-boy. They once almost had to force him to sign a paper swearing that he would deliver the message to his boss, the former minister.
While there are many others working for the department who hold these attitudes, there are many who have earned the respect of the Indian people; but it would appear that the department is top heavy with administrators who can deal only with non-people. I believe it would be of great benefit if we commissioned one of the financial houses of Toronto, which I understand are good at this kind of thing, to carry out a cost-benefit analysis of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. The department spends over $400 million of taxpayers' money on its Indian and Eskimo program. As a taxpayer, I often ask myself what benefit I receive from that money. As a native, I know the Indians receive very little.
The National Indian Brotherhood estimates there are about 40,000 Indian heads of households in Canada. If the government took the annual budget of the Indian Affairs program and divided it among those heads of households, each Indian family would receive about $10,000 a year. That would be a much better way to look after Indian
Indian Affairs
Affairs than spending the money to hire bureaucrats with whom the Indian people cannot communicate.
My time is running out. I could speak for several days about how this department and this minister hinder, rather than help, the Indian people. These people are administered, rather than allowed to take part as equals in Canadian society. I shall close by saying I support the motion now before the House, with one reservation. I wish the motion had called for the resignation of the minister and his top bureaucrats, and for the restructuring of a department which has completely lost touch with the task it has been given and now serves only the little kingdoms set up by its employees. I realize these are harsh words, but 1 mean every bit of what I am saying.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take part briefly in the debate brought about by the opposition and dealing with the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. The Minister of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Buchanan) may think there is no problem, but the opposition, at least some members and more especially the people concerned, feel as I do that in some respects there are problems.
The motion before us reads as follows:
That the House deplores the action of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development in moving toward policies of a paternalistic and bureaucratic nature with respect to native people and specifically requests that a moratorium be placed on the implementation of recent guidelines issued by the Department until such time as full consultation has taken place with the native people.
This is not the first time, I believe the matter has been brought to the attention of the House, perhaps not as a motion similar to this one, but at least as a form of protest not so much against the present Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development but, more particularly, against his predecessor.
Until now, too often decisions have been made with regard to Indian affairs without requesting their consent. And I remember very well that, at one point, the federal Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development was practically the only one who dealt with Indian and Eskimo affairs in Northern Quebec. Now, one day, along comes a little minister not too tall, named Rene Levesque, who decided, on behalf of the province of Quebec that the time had come for Quebec to look after all the citizens living within the boundaries of the province. Immediately, he took steps to impose certain things upon the department of Natural Resources, first at the level of Indian and Eskimo communities, not around but along the James Bay and Hudson Bay coastlines, as well as on the north side of the Hudson Strait, thus competing in a way with the federal government.
The Indians and Eskimos are in no way retarded or "innocents" as we say in French. In no time flat they understood to what advantage they could put that rivalry between the two governments and they tried in every possible way to benefit from it. Economically, I dare say, they succeeded to some extent. But one should wonder whether, over the long term, that has been advantageous.

June 12, 1975
Indian Affairs
The question we must ask today is whether the decisions that are made at either level of government, are always to the advantage of the natives. Have we always sought their opinion? Apparently, seeking their opinion is the last thing they would have thought of doing.
As early as 1968, at the 25th annual conference of the provincial ministers of mines, dealing with the fabulous future of mining in the North, the Quebec Minister of Natural Resources, Mr. Paul Allard, used the word "fabulous", but without saying for whom. However, we soon understood that Quebec's future would not be "fabulous" for the natives but for the multinationals. At that time, he made the following statement, quote:
As is taking shape the mining and industrial development of Northern Quebec which looks increasingly like a promising economic empire, it is our duty in this province to integrate the native population to our labour force-
"Integrate" the native population means change their outlook, their attitude, their behaviour, and bring them round to the point of view that we, the Whites-
-and to encourage the participation of Indians and Eskimos in this economic emancipation so that they may become first-class citizens.
How come that in the middle of the 20th century, Indians and Eskimos are not recognized as first-class Canadian citizens?
Those populations will have to be prepared for the role they are expected to play.
What "role" do we expect of them or did we expect them to play in 1968? It should be kept in mind, Madam Speaker, that 1968 was all the same a few years before premier Bourassa decided to develop the hydroelectric potential of this large area of James Bay. As we know, premier Bou-rassa's decision was taken without any consultation with the natives living in that area. They don't give a hoot about the opinion of the Canadian people and then they say: we must bring them round to our point of view, make them share in our decisions.
Later, during an important meeting at the Maison Montmorency, near Quebec City, where authorized representatives of the 26,000 or 27,000 Indians of Quebec were gathered, the fundamental rights of the Indian people were defined, and among these appear the following in particular:
The right of the Indian people to the status of nation.
Madam Speaker, "to obtain the status of nation" meant that at that time, the Indian people were aware of the fact that they were not recognized as a nation, recognition in principle of the right to self-government-
This is what the Indians demand, this is what they want. It is not separatism, far from it. It means that they want to take part in decision making, they want the right to discuss with the federal Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development or with his provincial counterpart. -native rights to reserve ownership,
-"ownership", I could add here real and not ficticious ownership.
and to the respect of their territorial rights-hunting and fishing rights-year round and everywhere.
Perhaps are we ready to recognize those rights. I am not speaking here for other provinces but for Quebec, and

particularly for the vast territory of New Quebec, the greater part of which in Abitibi I represent.
Even if their hunting and fishing rights are recognized year round, everywhere rivers and lakes are being depleted of their fish by the "big shots", from the United States or elsewhere, who come in droves and have no respect whatsoever for fishing regulations. Even if we recognize those rights to natives, if nothing remains, what is left for them?
Secondly, in the huge area which is being developed for hydroelectric power, we do not even know by now, even though the project is at a fairly advanced stage, the implications of such development on wild life, on fishes both in the rivers and in James Bay itself. Again, they did not bother to seek the opinion of the natives of the area.
They also want that their linguistic and cultural rights be recognized. An attempt is made to teach them English and French, but too often instruction in their own language, the language they need, is neglected. I have here a statement made by the Northwest Territories Commis-sionner in 1966, when he was in office. At a study session in an Ottawa normal school, he stated the following:
All primitive cultures are doomed to disappear.
That was the opinion of the Northwest Territories Commissioner. And he added:
Our form of civilization is the best that ever existed. Eskimos should feel darn lucky to be plunged in the North-American melting pot.
Such is the thinking of those Who must protect those people. Now, I think they sometimes have cause to worry. They also demand the right that the Indians Act or any other act affecting the Indians be not amended, without their consent. So let the minister never forget it. It is the Indians' wish.
Madam Speaker, too often we try to govern the natives as a conquered nation. It is our shortcoming. Can't we understand, in 1975, that the natives have, as a nation, rights that must be respected? Why must they live like us to be good Canadians? The farmers of the central provinces do not necessarily live as Matagami miners, nor do they necessarily lives as Maritimes fishermen, and yet they are good Canadians.
Now, if the Indians or the Eskimos want to live, to keep on living in their own way, why deny them that right and not accept them as good Canadians?
Madam Speaker, I think the minister should take note of those considerations and always keep them in mind. I believe there have been, particularly in recent years, a great improvement in that area, and I am quite sure the minister will outline them in his statement.
But there is still concern. Measures are passed but we do not know how to enforce them. Recently, a Federal-Provincial Conference on Native Peoples and the Criminal Justice System was held in Edmonton. During that conference, various points were made, particularly on the problem of alcoholism. The Quebec Minister of Justice made that remark about the liquor law in the Northwest Territories. Minister Choquette feels that law is a bit too restrictive. "It smacks of prohibition", he said. And when he sees prohibition, he immediately sees a black market.
June 12, 1975

If a locality, be it Fort Smith, Frobisher Bay, Fort Chimo or any other place, should impose prohibition, then Minister Choquette would not know how to enforce that decision. It is truly regrettable to see a parliament pass pieces of legislation, and then, it is impossible to implement them. We see that almost every day.
We just saw, during the long trial of Dr. Morgentaler, that an act of the federal Parliament exists and that a jury can very well evade and flout it. So, I wonder if we should not quite simply abolish Parliament and have measures passed by groups of 10 or 12 people that would be called jurors.
Madam Speaker, I may have strayed somewhat from the point but in conclusion I want to come back to the motion introduced by the opposition and urge the Minister of Indian Affairs (Mr. Buchanan) to see to it that his officials-and I am convinced that he is very well-intentioned at the helm of his department-indeed respect the mentality of the people he wants to administer, but let him consult them as often as possible. Before taking any major decision or bringing any major bill before the House, he should make sure that all concerned were consulted.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext:
Just a couple of days ago I was chatting with one of the senior people in the Union of New Brunswick Indians and again the same message came through. They had some particular concerns about them. They said, in effect: "Generally, we welcome the spelling out of these guidelines so that we know exactly where we stand and so that our various bands know what requirements will be put upon them."
Concern has also been expressed about the authority of band councils. Part of the confusion results from use of the term "local government authority" as used in the guidelines. If one reads "band council" instead of "local government authority", the confusion will disappear. We intend, as I said, to reinforce the responsibilities of the band council, which is the predominant group in the band. We feel we ought to reinforce it. I feel I ought to emphasize that point because of the concern expressed by the Indian people: we intend to reinforce the council.
Concern was also expressed about district councils. Again, I wish to make it clear that in a case where a band decides to establish a district council, the council derives all authority and responsibility from the band which decided to form it. The district council has no powers of its own. All the powers it possesses are those which are given to it by the various bands making up the district. In some areas of Canada, particularly in British Columbia, this concept works very well. In other areas people are concerned that perhaps the district concept represents an undermining of the band itself. I therefore wish to emphasize that a band can join the district council at any time, and it can withdraw from that council at any time and decide to conduct its own affairs. That is the second area about which concern has been expressed to us.
As for the suggestion that we are trying to belittle the authority of the band council, let me say unequivocally in this House that the very opposite is true. We have no desire whatsoever to undermine the authority of the band council. We say that these guidelines will help to reinforce the authority of the band council and emphasize its predominant role in the operation of the band. The various sub-authorities, such as the housing authority which was mentioned earlier, derive their powers from the band council and are responsible to the band council. I emphasize, we do not intend to undermine the responsibility or actual authority of the band council in the handling of its own affairs.
Other concerns of a more detailed nature have been raised. There is the question of tender limits which the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Malone) has raised in this House on other occasions. We have already made changes in that area and we are prepared, particularly in the more remote areas, to look at the necessity of additional changes.
It has been suggested that quarterly audited statements are required. Such a requirement would be more onerous than the requirement the Department of National Revenue places on corporations for filing annual tax returns: quarterly audited statements are not required; we expect them

June 12, 1975
Indian Affairs
on an annual basis, not each quarter. Concern has been expressed about certain details of the guidelines. We think, by and large, that these will work themselves out as officials meet various bands, discuss the guidelines and endeavour to impart a better understanding of how they are to function.
If I may digress, I note some confusion about the concept of consultation. I received a report of a recent meeting at which the friend of the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth), the Premier of Manitoba, discussed for a few minutes with Indian bands and others present the meaning of consultation. He made it clear that "consultation" means exactly that: you consult; you obtain opinions. He said it does not mean that the government is to abdicate its reponsibility in making the ultimate decision. In other words, consultation does not mean that some group outside the government, be it the Indian people or any other group, has the right to make the final decision and say, "Government, you must implement that decision." That responsibility rests on the government. I mention the point because it is interesting and because the Premier of Manitoba saw fit to raise it and discuss it at a meeting which he attended recently.
As far as reinforcing the authority of Indian groups and holding discussions with Indian groups at the band, district, provincial or federal level, I suggest that no government in the history of our country has done more to develop and encourage the development of Indian organizations than has the government of which I have the honour to be a member. Ten years ago most Indian organizations across this country found it difficult to articulate their views or even come together and make their views known. Now, Indian organizations of this country are quite capable of putting their views across. But for the encouragement and assistance the federal government has given to our Indian organizations, those organizations would not be in a position to make their views known so well and hon. members on both sides of the House would be unaware of the concerns which have been articulated today.

Although my predecessor was often on the receiving end of much criticism levelled at him by this House and by the Indian people of Canada, he deserves credit for a major accomplishment. His work led to the development of the policy which enabled the Indian people of our country to stand up, say what they think and say what their rights are. That was a significant accomplishment in the field of relations with our Indian people.
I return to the theme of some, that we are not listening to the Indian people. Some suggest that the work of the department leaves much to be desired. It has been suggested by the Union of B.C. Indian Chiefs that the department should wind down, diminish its services.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development

speechtext:
I have said that we are quite prepared to discuss whether this should be done and how it should be done. There is no suggestion that we are not willing to sit down and discuss with the Indian people changes in the

functioning of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and cutting back the services provided by the department. I find that there is interest in such cutbacks on the one hand, but, on the other hand, when I attended an all-chiefs' meeting in Ontario not long ago a major petition presented to me took strong exception to the closing of some departmental offices. We cannot have it both ways. If we are to turn over more services to the Indian people, if they are to handle more services directly, without doubt we will need to cut back on our staff and the number of offices and facilities which we run.
An indication of our willingness to turn over responsibility to the Indian people for the running of their own affairs is the fact that ten years ago Indian organizations, bands and Innuit settlements throughout the country were handling and administering roughly $60,000 in federal funds, but now they are handling close to $100 million. That fact hardly shows that the government is not prepared to give responsibility to the Indian people.
