speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext:
Much of the theme that ran through the comments of the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes) was-and I have this written down-the total rejection of the right to local autonomy. That is simply not true. As I indicated, if one looks at the arithmetic it is pretty hard to square that accusation with the fact that the government has now given responsibility for the administration of funds, whether in education, social welfare or other areas, to the Indian people to the tune of $100 million as opposed to $60,000 ten years ago. I suggest that is a far cry from total rejection of the right to local autonomy.
The thrust we would like to have is the reinforcement of local autonomy and reinforcing the responsibility of the band council. That is the major desire in these guidelines, to help give a framework, which they set out. We are quite prepared to make changes. In fact, we have already made changes, some minor, such as the amount required as far as tendering is concerned. We are prepared to make these changes, and I think that is extremely important.
I take strong exception to the fact that the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth) indulged in a personal attack on employees of the department. As far as I

June 12, 1975

am concerned, that is a very bad practice. The hon. member can attack me all he wants; that is why I am here. However, he should not attack individuals in the department who have no way of responding or defending themselves. It is a long-standing practice in the House of Commons that that is not done. You can attack the minister as vigorously as you wish, but do not go after the employees in the department.
The hon. member referred to Jim Wright who moved into Saskatchewan under very difficult circumstances. He was brought in to straighten out administrative difficulties in the province of Saskatchewan. We made it clear to the Federation of Saskatchewan Indians that we will welcome their sitting on the panel for the selection of a permanent regional director in the province of Saskatchewan. Mr. Wright was to be there on an interim basis. We moved him in because the situation required fast action. I find it most regrettable that the hon. member for Northwest Territories would attack public servants in this House.
The hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise) dwelt at some length on the right and the wish of the native people of Canada to govern themselves, to have a greater say in managing their own affairs. I can only reiterate what I said to the hon. member for Lambton-Kent and the hon. member for Northwest Territories, that we share this desire. We are quite prepared, with proper guidelines, to turn over to the Indian people as much responsibility for their affairs as possible. As far as I am concerned, that is a fundamental cornerstone of our policy, whether it is the management of funds or running the various other aspects that apply directly to their lives. We feel strongly that that should be the thrust. Certainly there will be mistakes made. Lord knows, we have made more than our share. I am surprised that remark went by without comment. I have no doubt there that mistakes will be made, but we think that is a small price to pay to increase the independence and self-reliance of the native people of this country.
The hon. member for Northwest Territories referred to the departmental task force which was set up in 1972. As he indicated, it held 28 meetings across the country with band councils, some provincial Indian associations and departmental staff. A report of its findings was released in April, 1973, and sent to all bands and provincial associations. The recommendations emanating from those findings centred mainly around the need for core funding for band councils, the need to lay a sound and lasting basis for local government on reserves and, finally, the need for local government guidelines. I quote recommendations 5, 6, 7 and 8 which relate directly to the production of the guidelines:
5.	Bands should carry out their own planning, establishing their own priorities and controlling their own O and M and capital budgets. A contractual agreement that stipulates the authorities and responsibilities on both parties is required.
6.	A manual of local government guidelines written for band staff should be developed by Indian Affairs in consultation with band councils. It should embody good business principles used by all types of organizations in several fields; personnel, finances, contracts, purchasing, general administration, etc.
Indian Affairs
7.	The manual of local government guidelines should also clarify the roles of:
-Chief and council
-Band staff
-Department of Indian Affairs staff concerning-
(i)	Authority
(ii)	Responsibility
(iii)	Accountability
8.	Bookkeeping procedures need to be:
-standardized;
-simplified;
-a bookkeeper/trainer available on the job to teach the day to day operations of office procedures and financial management. Band records are generally poor.
I should say that in addition to the task force recommendations we have been asked fairly often at all-chiefs' meetings to produce guidelines which band staff could use in their day to day work. Chiefs have also expressed the need for some kind of regulations against which the auditor could measure the band's performance over the year. The program circulars prepared recently reflect an initial departmental response to the need for rules by which band business will be managed. I have probably dealt with that in sufficient detail. Those were the proposals of recommendations made as the result of the work of that task force. We feel these guidelines recommend a sound thrust. They reflect the desires that grew out of that task force report.
Before resuming my seat, I want again to emphasize that we are prepared to listen to suggestions for modification. We will listen to any ideas the native people may have concerning changes. I have indicated in this House on several occasions-this was indicated when the hon. member for Lambton-Kent was quoting some of my comments-that we look upon these guidelines as being of an interim nature. We are prepared to make changes. We regard the guidelines as a vehicle to clarify and reinforce the role of the band council. We want to make certain it is the supreme body on the reserve and has the major responsibility for operating the band's affairs.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext: Frankly, Madam Speaker, I am somewhat disappointed with the minister's comments. I hope he will take the opportunity later to set straight a couple of things he said in his speech that are of concern to me and should be of concern to all my colleagues. He made but one reference to a group of natives who had been consulted with regard to the guidelines we have been discussing this afternoon. The minister said the guidelines had been established to reinforce the authority of the band councils. In saying this he implied that the guidelines were intended to break down the authority of the regional councils. In some areas, he said, these councils performed a worth-while function but in others they did not. He said, in effect, that he wanted to get in between the regional councils-

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext: District councils.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext:
-the district councils and the band councils so as to reinforce the authority of the band councils. I cannot help wondering whether the minister is becoming

June 12, 1975
Indian Affairs
somewhat afraid of the way in which these district councils have learned to articulate the case of the Indians in this country. I hope the minister will retract that statement of his and not leave the impression that he is concerned about the increasing influence of the Union of Indian Chiefs, for example, or the Union of B.C. Indian Chiefs. That is what he implied. Perhaps I misunderstood the hon. gentleman, but I believe the record will show that this is clearly what he implied.
The minister quoted the Premier of Manitoba as being an authority on the interpretation of the consultation process. He should probably have called it a consensus process, because he used that authority to say, "Sure, we will go out and consult; but it will be the government which implements things regardless of what the consultation process brings to light." In the case we are discussing there was no consultation. The minister knows this and so does everybody else who will be taking part in the debate.
It will be a test of one's imagination to speculate on how many hours, how many days have passed in debate in this chamber on Indian affairs over the years. I often think the real reason no progress has ever been made as a result of all these debates is the fact that the native tongue has never been heard in this chamber, and that if it had, its vocabulary would not be adequate to articulate the plight, the persecution and the injustices we have perpetrated against the native people of North America.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext: No one would have understood them anyway.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext:
It is only in the most recent years that the native people in sufficient number have learned to express their feelings and their frustrations in our languages, and at last their message has been brought to this chamber. Unfortunately, however, it has too often been carried by messengers only, people who could not understand the depth of the problem or demonstrate real concern about the plight of those affected. Even today we still argue about the interpretation of phrases like "aboriginal rights" or "aboriginal title." While we are carrying out this exercise, we are building up the frustration of the native people in the face of our system.
As our ancestors moved across the continent, intruding on the way of life of its inhabitants, they often sent out scouts to monitor the moves of the Indians so as to be prepared to respond to trouble or resistance. I felt like such a scout recently when I travelled to British Columbia to attend the meetings of the Union of British Columbia Indian Chiefs, trying to learn about their problems, or when I travelled to Prince Edward Island last weekend where another group of natives called the Non-Status Indian Association of the Native Council of Canada was holding its annual assembly.
Madam Speaker, I think it is fair to report, as scouts of an earlier era have often reported, that the natives are restless. They are restless and frustrated because of the way in which pleas for recognition of their rights have been ignored. Natives everywhere are angered by the way in which treaties have been ignored and fractured. They tell me that at least 75 per cent of the 22,000 reservations and land holdings in Canada have been intruded upon in some way, offending the trust they had placed in the

contract made with the Great White Father. They are angered over the retrograde steps taken recently by the present administration and the ignorance displayed by the Minister of Indian Affairs (Mr. Buchanan) and his most senior officials.
Our reason for postponing debate on this subject until today was mainly to allow the minister, who assumed office only last year, to become familiar with his tasks. We have ignored some of the earlier mistakes the hon. gentleman made, in the hope he would learn from experience. After all, he was not entirely new to the job; he served- and may I say he served well-as chairman of the committee on Indian affairs for two years prior to his appointment. But time is running on and we feel it is fair, now, to ask him to account for his actions. We also feel that members of parliament and the native people of Canada are entitled to know how he intends to carry out his mandate and how he proposes to deal with the special rights our native people possess.
Frankly, Madam Speaker, my colleagues and I are not at all impressed by the minister's performance so far. He appears to us like a man who did not bring to his job his own ideas or his own commitments. He appears to be following guidelines which others before him established and which are out of tune with the needs of today. He allows too free a hand in the administration of day to day affairs to those who have managed or, one might better say, mismanaged those affairs for the past 100 years, namely, the Department of Indian Affairs and all its bureaucrats, technocrats and officials most of whom are well known to be much too preoccupied with serving their own self-interests.
It should come as no surprise that on April 24 of this year the Union of B.C. Indian Chiefs passed a resolution calling upon all Indians in the province to reject, as of May 1, funds from all federal departments and agencies including, of course, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. Subsequently, a number of Indian representatives called upon the department to transfer to them the management of funds in British Columbia. In response to this resolution, the minister stated:
I have responded positively to these proposals. The expressed wish of Indians in B.C. to reduce their dependence on the government, to stress self-reliance and to assume substantially greater responsibility for the management of their own affairs corresponds very closely with my own objectives not merely in respect of Indians in British Columbia but in all parts of Canada.
If one really analyses what the minister intended to say to the Indians of British Columbia following upon their resolution, the answer appears in the pages of the guidelines and regulations which, if not complied with would, he said, result in the withholding of all or any funds from federal sources. The guidelines are a terrible example of what I referred to earlier. Only a technocrat of the highest order could have invented such a schemozzle. How on earth could the average Indian band possibly fulfil the requirements of these guidelines? It would take the services, on a regular basis, of a chartered accountant trained in extra skills such as administration not only of economic activities but also of social programs, educational programs, municipal accounting, and so on.
June 12, 1975

There is, of course, no one person who will be able to acquire all these skills, so each band will engage the services of a municipal administrator, a social programs administrator and an educational administrator. Perhaps what the department wants to achieve with these guidelines is full employment for all Indians under their care. Each band member will get a full salary for filling out a report of his entire activities during each day-and I am not even being facetious when I say that.
I should like to refer to some statistics that have been provided to me by the minister's department. We have a total registered Indian population of 275,000. Of that number, 75,000 between the ages of 16 and 64 could be considered as belonging to the labour force, and 40,000 are working, giving an unemployment rate of 40 per cent. Of these 75,000, only 15,802 are employed in industries such as farming, forestry fishing and tourism. Incidentally, all of these industries are, of course, of a very seasonal nature. The other 24,200 are listed as being employed in social services, band management and community work programs.
Perhaps, Madam Speaker, the minister's officials have already made the decision that each band should operate like the department of Indian affairs. You create enough work to keep everybody busy administering himself and his friends, and all problems will be solved. Well, the Indians are not so naive as to fall for this primitive prank. They interpret this measure to be yet another ball and chain that they would be required to carry around, as yet another shackle tying them to the apron strings of the Indian agent.
The minister is again speaking with forked tongue when he says he is willing to pass on some more of the responsibility to the Indian people; that he will help them achieve greater self-reliance. If he were really serious about that, he would have consulted with native leaders regarding the establishment of these guidelines. If he had been serious, would he not have insisted that some discretion be applied by his officials, particularly in some area where significant achievements in the field of socio-economic development have already been made, where native communities are already spending only those funds that they themselves have generated as a result of such activities? But no, there was no consultation because there could be no consultation-in a meaningful way, anyway-under the present system.
Like all other bureaucratic monsters, the Indian affairs department is no exception. The more cumbersome it gets, the greater the desire for a simple, over-all application of their programs. After all, it must have taken all their ingenuity, resources and capacity to procrastinate, to come up with this octopus-like brainchild. It is a truly bureaucratic achievement and surely it must be good for everybody! It caused quite an uproar throughout the country when the first print, together with the minister's letter telling individual bands that unless they lived by these guidelines no further funds would be available, arrived at the offices of the band councils. One of the leaders in B.C. told me, "It stinks, and we will not comply". It is as simple as that, Madam Speaker, and I for one respect that view.
Indian Affairs
It is this document that caused all the uproar, at least in British Columbia, that prompted the Union of B.C. Chiefs to pass a resolution not to accept any further funds from the department; because the minister's letter raised, again, the questions that have been asked ever since the Indian Act was written, namely, "Whose money is the minister spending, anyway? Whose money is he withholding if we don't comply with the guidelines?" They say it is their money. Not only do they wish in the future to determine their own destiny and how much their annual budget requirements will be; they also want to determine how the money will be spent and what the priorities are.
Where do these people find the courage-or, as some would say, the audacity-to talk to the minister like this? From the lack of leadership and courage by the present government, resulting in the intervention of our judicial system in some instances of disputes over land claims and other special rights. The books were opened and the old treaties re-examined by legal minds. It was then discovered that the four Hudson's Bay blankets, the ammunition, the medicine chest and the $5 per family per month was to be compensation for only an interim period during which natives could be helped to adjust, develop their own economic activities for which opportunities would be provided, and to establish a value for the land they had surrendered to their white brothers.
We all know today that it was unfortunate that we did not sooner concern ourselves with this obligation, which today remains unfulfilled. Perhaps we could have negotiated a price at the time that could have been similar to what the United States paid for the island of Manhattan, or what they paid the Russians for what is now the state of Alaska.
Values have, of course, changed and are measured by much different standards today. Not only would a cash settlement of land claims be in many billions of dollars, but we also find ourselves, since no settlement has yet been achieved, in the interim period of adjustment to which the treaties make reference. This means that by today's standards the Hudson's Bay blanket which was to provide shelter is now interpreted to be a house; the medicine chest has become access to hospitals; the ammunition and the $5 cash allowance translates into a subsistence allowance of modern-day standards.
So you see, Madam Speaker, it is becoming abundantly clear that the central issue is the settlement of land claims. We are critical of the minister because, while a feeble effort has been made to allow Indians to identify their claims, there is no suggestion as to how these claims are to be settled. We believe that even at this late date it is possible to achieve a settlement by consultation and negotiation rather than by the judicial process, and we feel that negotiated settlements would better serve the interests of all concerned.
There is, however, no doubt in my mind that the Indians will no longer negotiate with officials of the Indian affairs department. One hundred years of failure and of broken promises is too much of a test even for the Indians and they are now demanding to bring their case directly to the cabinet and the privy council. This is why the natives of British Columbia have decided to cut the apron strings and to split their sheets, so to speak. They have never

June 12, 1975
Indian Affairs
resisted accountability, but they now insist it is time the minister accounted as well. They are telling the minister that they will no longer allow moneys rightfully belonging to them to be spent in ways not at all to do with the things for which they are kept in trust, but to ease the horrendous burden of the white man's conscience.
The Indians in British Columbia feel-and I detect a mood of unrest throughout the country-that it is time to call the Great White Father back to the negotiating table. The Great White Mother must be represented by the privy council this time, as the Indians feel it is time to remind the white man of the words he has spoken over the last 200 years. It is not their intention to have their brothers and sisters any longer branded with words like "status", "nonstatus", "registered" and "non-registered", or branded with the welfare stigma. They say:
If you want accountability, we agree, but we want our guidelines implemented at the same time as we adhere to yours. If you insist on concise terms of our guidelines, we will provide you with them.
They will include reconciliation of moneys flowing from your public purse, with our aboriginal rights and our claims against the lands which you have taken from us.
It will be us in the future who will tell you what our budget requirements will be and, indeed, what our priorities will be in the future. If you feel that we are overdrawing our account, it should be an incentive to you to audit the books and reconcile the account. In order to do that, however, you will have to be serious with us about negotiating or adjudicating our claims.
Unless the minister does that, he will not know whether the account is overdrawn. This is the message I received in talking to our native people; and I know that the minister, too, has interpreted the murmur of the distant drums. It is timely for him and his colleagues to once more smoke the pipe, to once more consult before he insists on the implementation of these ridiculous guidelines.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am quite please to take part in the debate on an opposition motion deploring the fact that the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has not fully consulted the native people before drawing up and issuing guidelines on the structures and financing of band councils and Innuit villages.
Madam Speaker, I have been a member of the Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development for over seven years. I had the opportunity to sit on that committee when the minister was chairman for a few years, and I can say that the committee has given close attention to the requests of the native people.
It is our committee I think that examined and considered the requests that were made, either before or after they were conveyed to the minister or regional directors. And the committee members inquired into the situation existing on the reserves, and even in the far North. We were able on many occasions to make suggestions to the Cabinet and ministers, and several of them have now, so to speak, become realities.
Our committee went down to meet the administration councils on many reserves. I will admit that the current

problems brought to our attention by the native community are quite complex. Often they even vary from one area to another and one province to another. However, I must say that no government in the past has paid so much attention to Indian, Innuit and Eskimo claims. Task forces were set up, one of which to study Indian claims, headed by Mr. Barber. Then, under the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development who was chairman at the time, the committee sat for six months in 1973 and heard evidence on the question of "native rights". Furthermore, many assistance and funding programs were brought forward by this government in order to allow our native people to administer themselves some projects or undertakings of their choice.
Coming back to the guidelines issued by the department on local administration for band councils and Innuit villages the minister in a press release dated June 2, 1975, stated the following:
Reaction from provincial and national Indian leaders has been outspoken. Fears have been expressed that, through these guidelines, the department has devised a way to enable it to tax Indians; amend the Indian Act without consultation; undermine the authority of chiefs and councillors; resurrect the 1969 White Paper; or all four.
The department points out that the five guidelines are limited to the structure and funding of local government. They provide for minimal but essential accounting and auditing requirements, delineate responsibilities and, generally speaking, describe the parameters of departmental funding for the many programs involved. Each contains a clause soliciting suggestions for amendments from Indian bands and Innuit settlements and staff alike.
Madam Speaker, when issuing regulations or guidelines, no level of government, whether it be federal, provincial or municipal, no department, no union leader can please everyone. Some people will always be dissatisfied with regulations and legislation but when you do not make decisions you cannot be criticized. This government together with the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development take position and that is why they are criticized.
Madam Speaker, this government is a decision maker and I am convinced that Canadians are satisfied.
To come back to the guidelines of the motion, I wish to refer to the Debates of the House of Commons of May 6th when the minister stated; "We are prepared to regard these guidelines as being of an interim nature. If they create difficulties and problems, we are prepared to change them."
Madam Speaker, I wish that today's proceedings will throw some light on some of the problems raised by the new guidelines and that the constructive suggestions put forward by my good friends of the opposition as well as those from the members on the government side will enable the minister to bring about some changes if he deems it necessary.
Hon. members recognize that Indians need freedom to achieve their cultural, economic and social fulfilment within the Canadian society. As a matter of fact, the department supports the creation of organizations for the autonomy of bands and villages. This is also the reason why the local autonomy program was created and expands rapidly. Most Indian bands are now responsible for the
Indian Affairs
implementation of various programs. Earlier this week, we have seen the successful results obtained in the Huron village near Quebec City.
The Committee on the Indian Affairs and Northern Development which I chair, earlier this week visited the Huron village near Quebec City. I can tell you that we have been amazed at the success of the undertakings promoted under the program of the government of Canada.
In the Huron village, manufacturers hire all the workers available on the reserve and chief Mac Gros-Louis told us that he even uses white people from outside the reserve. He also told us that only sick people were on welfare. The local authorities of this reserve took their responsibilities, and the drive of these businessmen was the main reason for the development of that village of 1,200 people.
Madam Speaker, development also depends on the quality and the discipline of all the workers. We have noted that all the directors on the reserve, under the artful leadership of chief, Mac Gros-Louis, feel confident in the economic future of the reserves, because they believe first in the will and determination of the Indians themselves to make it a success.
The Huron village sets an example for all native people in Canada. This does not mean it is the only thriving reservation in Canada, because numerous others enjoy advanced industrial and commercial development.
As elsewhere, some Indian endeavours fail and others succeed, but I believe it is worthwhile to try.
The former Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, now President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien), had this to say when promoting local government, and I quote;
Local government will in no way endanger the system of reservations, Indian status, nor the funds, services and programs provided by the Canadian government. Quite the contrary, I firmly believe that local government is vitally needed to allow Indians to keep their way of life, their identity and pride and to really participate in Canadian life.
As the minister stated, such is still the department's policy, and I believe we should at least give the minister and his officials an opportunity to implement the principles set forth a few months ago for the government of Indian and Innuit reservations and councils in Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to speak on this very important motion today because it concerns the first people of our country. This year, 1975, marks the one-hundredth anniversary of Winnipeg Treaty No. 5. In this centennial year I would ask the minister to consider an increase in the $5 treaty payment now being made-because of the one-hundredth anniversary of Treaty No. 5. While the minister referred to Treaty No. 7, and to the people covered by that treaty as being very able and competent, I want to say that the people covered by Treaty No. 5 are just as able and competent and their treaty was signed quite a few years earlier than Treaty No. 7.
I wish to touch on the educational facilities and the problems the Indian people have concerning Indian control of education. I would give a little of the background in

June 12, 1975
Indian Affairs
this regard. The previous minister, on May 24, 1973, reported to the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development that his department was ready to implement an education policy formulated by the National Indian Brotherhood. Under this policy, Indian control over Indian education would follow closely the 17 recommendations for improving Indian education which the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development tabled in the House on June 22, 1971. The previous minister stated:
I have given the National Indian Brotherhood my assurance that I and my department are fully committed to realizing the educational goals for the Indian people which are set forth in the brotherhood's proposal.
The department desires to work constructively with the Indian communities on a partnership basis which encourages full, free and frank discussion and which places a major responsibility for educational decisions and directions in the hands of the Indian community concerned. The department's role will increasingly become that of a service function to which bands can turn if they feel the need for consultation, for discussions, and for the provision of specialized educational services; however, the control and responsibility-
I want to emphasize this point.
-will rest with the bands to chart their educational course, seeking whatever assistance they require from whatever source they desire.
When the minister made that statement I am sure he was aware of the problems which people in the remote communities face so far as education is concerned. I think' it is almost impossible to come up with a blanket policy to cover every Indian community across Canada and that it would be necessary to look at each individual case. Every community is different; they are at different stages of development, and so on. I believe that in attempting to implement something like this, we must look at the guidelines set up by the National Indian Brotherhood.
The word "consultation" was mentioned in the previous minister's statement. I want to assure you, Mr. Speaker, that consultation with the people responsible for the educational branch of the National Indian Brotherhood involved merely the odd meeting and discussion with a few individuals. In the eyes of the Indian people, it is not consultation when it involves speaking to only a few people. Their interpretation of "consultation" is sitting down and discussing the entire problem at length, not having a very short, interim type of discussion.
The discrepancies between what is being said and what is being done will shock, I am sure, even the most casual observer. On the one hand, there is the policy on Indian education which was approved by the former minister of Indian affairs and northern development in his statement in the House on May 24. On the other hand, there are the rejected band council resolutions and the withdrawal of services and funds formerly supplied by the department.
At present, many implications can be drawn from the educational policy implemented by public servants which is derived from the white paper policy on Indian affairs of 1969, and not from the policy paper on Indian control of Indian education presented in 1972. The minister promised that Indian parents would be partners with department officials, implying consultation and shared responsibility. This promise, in fact, has not been honoured.

I could go on giving examples such as this Mr. Speaker, but I know that my time is limited. My main concern is with educational assistance to reserve Indians. This is the real concern of the National Indian Brotherhood. The previous minister accepted a policy which stated that the federal government is financially responsible for providing education to all status Indians whether living on or off reserves. This has not been the practice of the department. It is generally understood by district, regional and headquarters' officials that Indians living off reserves are no longer the responsibility of the federal government. In this case it is the treaties, not the Indian Act, that are being interpreted by the public servants. The authority for doing this should be examined, as well as the negotiations between federal and provincial officials during which this policy was established.
Recent recommendations made by the regional directors show a determination to phase out Indian Affairs services to off-reserve Indians. I think this situation is discriminatory, for the simple reason that if a treaty Indian chooses to move off the reserve and obtain education elsewhere, that is part of his heritage and his right under Treaty No. 5 signed 100 years ago.
I am certainly concerned, also, about the priorities that are determined by public servants. The pressure on regional directors to reduce costs and control budgets has resulted in cuts to programs which are considered by the department as non-essential or of low priority. Among these are adult education, lunch supplements, band staffing, school supplies, library services, placement and relocation, student residences, and so on. The department has also listed its high priorities. These may not coincide with the priorities of the Indian communities in terms of their particular goals for local development.
Indian participation in determining priorities is usually limited, so that it becomes a negative and frustrating exercise. Indian control over local programs is achieved only after confrontation and struggle. I think that is a deplorable situation. Let me refer to the local school committees which are assigned the menial task of looking after school lunches or helping with some small program within the school. They are not part of the team which makes up the policy for the education of their children. They would like to be partners in this program, but they are not consulted as they should be.
What the Indian people really feel-and I have the opportunity to speak to large numbers of status Indians covered by Treaty No. 5-is that the department has put out a set of guidelines for education and has said, "You have had no part in setting up these guidelines but they are the guidelines you must follow, and if you do not follow them you will have no part of them". This is what people are complaining about. Sometimes a community has its own interpretation of the guidelines and they want to take part in setting them. When they made their proposals in 1972, the guidelines were set down. I do not feel the department has really taken a serious look at them. They had a preconceived idea as to how the guidelines should be drawn up.
I understand, also, that the minsiter has appointed a director of operations to administer the guidelines. This public servant has gone out to every region in Canada and


June 12, 1975

hand-picked the men and women who will work under him. I call these people whom he has hand-picked real hard-liners, the type of people who are not sympathetic to Indians: they are out there strictly as administrators. I can see another bureaucracy being set up and taking authority away from the Indian people, the chief and council. I deplore a situation such as this, because I know that after 100 years these people are prepared to take on responsibility and be accountable for their actions: there is no doubt about that.
I would like to emphasize, also, that local control of schools in various communities is a very important part of the education of Indian people across Canada. You should see how some of the local people apply themselves in spite of the fact that they receive no remuneration for their efforts. I know many people in the communities who are active on school committees in the belief that they have some authority. In fact, they have no authority, for the simple reason that no one is paying any attention to them.
We have spoken about priorities. The native people have a set of priorities which may be related to the local official; but they never get to the minister, as they should. That is one of the problems of the native people. In conclusion, I would like to voice very strongly, along with the Indian groups, opposition to the imposition of departmental guidelines. The minister should have his officials reconsider their intention to have the new policy circulars operative in 1975.
The alternative, as expressed by Indian leaders, is to continue with the guidelines which have been in effect until such time as full consultation and agreement can be reached on new operating procedures. This means a freeze on the circulars in series D and E which already have Treasury Board approval. It means extending the lead time for expected changes. The purpose of this action, which should clearly be understood by all concerned, is to arrive at mutually acceptable plans for the delivery of services and programs to Indian people. These should be based on Indian experience, focusing on band autonomy and local control, while emphasizing the funding and advisory role of the department.
I think we have to take this question into very serious consideration because it is what people in the outlying areas and out on the reserves are saying: they want a freeze to be placed on this. They are not all saying just throw it out, but they want a freeze put on it and they want to play the very important part of being on the team, or being partners as referred to by the previous minister. They want to be partners, but they want to be equal partners.
The minister referred to an article in the Kainai News but he neglected to quote part of the article. He read the part which sounded good from his side, but at the bottom of the page he did not go into guidelines which were opposed at the conference. That portion was nicely blanked out. Incidentally, the minister provided us with this document but that portion was blanked out. I still do not know what was actually included, but I would appreciate obtaining a copy of it, because it was not all one-sided.
Indian Affairs
Speaking of consultation, I must also bring to the attention of the House the problem some communities are having with regard to construction of school facilities. In many communities school facilities are in a deplorable condition and the people in those communities are trying desperately to improve conditions. What is really happening is that contracts are being let and designs of schools are being developed with little or no input by the local people. They are complaining, and justly so, that facilities are put in, moneys are spent and they have no say whatsoever as to the type of facility that is required. All of a sudden a building plan arrives and the people are told that construction will begin within six months, but they have little or no say in this and they are not part of the over-all education program.
We must also put our efforts toward alcohol education. That is what local control is going to provide, because local control has very clearly spelled out, in its policy paper on Indian control of Indian education, the very serious problem with alcohol education on the reserves. While the minister does have a small program which covers alcohol education, I do not believe it is extensive enough because alcohol is one of the most serious problems on many northern reserves. This is brought about by utter frustration on the part of the people who live in remote areas, for the simple reason that they have no input. The consultation process is just a case of speaking to a few people and obtaining opinions-sometimes not even as many as ten people-from a particular settlement or reserve. This is a deplorable situation.
I am definitely opposed to the way the guidelines have been implemented and I am sure that my colleagues will be touching on the very serious matters which have arisen from the implementation of these guidelines. I would not hesitate for one minute to say that if these guidelines are to be forced down the throats of the Indian people, we will probably see some violence. Hopefully not; but I think we might see something more than that witnessed here last fall at the opening of parliament. I hope that that day will never come again, because the Indian people have obeyed the treaties they have had for 100 years. They are looking to us for some help, but the existing guidelines are more of a hindrance than a help.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I could perhaps have made a more professional and a better contribution to this important debate if I could have consulted in my mother tongue, which is French, the guidelines issued. Unfortunately, these guidelines have not yet been published in both official languages, and I found it difficult to look fully into them, just as certain bands from Quebec probably found it difficult to study them in depth and to voice their opinion about them to their representatives in the House of Commons.
The debate in which I have the privilege to take part today is extremely important because, as far as I can understand, these guidelines have not yet been finalized and there is still room for improvement. Indeed, this is what the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Buchanan) stated today in his speech, as he had already done several times, and more particularly in the House, when he said that these guidelines were of

June 12, 1975
Indian Affairs
an interim nature and that he and his officials were prepared to change them if their implementation in the reservations created problems.
Even though this debate is very important, and I am grateful to the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes) for having raised the subject at this time in the House of Commons, I am surprised by the wording of his motion, because he uses, as his party is wont to do, a bombastic language with references to paternalism and dirigisme or bureaucracy as concerns the Indian affairs policy.
One day, they say that our defence policy is bureaucratic and paternalistic, the next day, the same is said about the Indian affairs policy, later about the unemployment insurance policy, and, Mr. Speaker, one could name any matter which concerns this nation and our friends opposite will always accuse us of dirigisme and paternalism, like a broken record.
This seems to me all the more surprising that after having had the pleasure for one year to sit on the Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development, I always found with my colleagues opposite and my Liberal colleagues such a spirit of understanding and an openness of mind on that committee that the subjects we had to deal with, more particularly matters of Indian policy, are of deepest concern to all of us because we are not, except for my hon. colleague for Kamloops-Cariboo (Mr. Marchand) and my hon. colleague from the Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth) very familiar with the problems facing natives across Canada. It is always with an openness of mind and a lot of respect that we listened, not with partisanship but as representatives of the Canadian electorate, to the various witnesses who came to meet us and always tried to find solutions to all problems in a spirit of co-operation. I say this, Mr. Speaker, simply to show my surprise on noting the somewhat bombastic wording of the motion of my colleague, the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes).
So, the fear of Indian, Innuit and Eskimo leaders across Canada, as well as the fear of some of my colleagues with regard to the guidelines just issued stems from a fear, Mr. Speaker, that through those guidelines, the Indians would be subject to taxation or that the act would be changed without consultation, or that the authority of chiefs and councillors would be undermined, or still that the famous white paper of 1969 would be brought forward again.
When one takes a closer look at what the guidelines concerning the structures and funding of band councils and Innuit villages are, one sees that they deal exclusively with the structures and funding of local administration. So I think there is nothing there to worry about and no need, as certain previous speakers did, to play the prophets of doom and talk about the possibility of violence following the implementation of those guidelines, or still take advantage of this debate to deal with claims over lands that happen to be owned by certain Indian bands, because this has nothing to do with the guidelines before us today. One of the previous speakers even referred to abortion, a matter which is totally irrelevant.
It seems that, as usual, they want to deal once again with the form instead of the substance of the bill. They

say that the bands have not been consulted. But they never say on what they should have been consulted.
That is why I should like to dwell for some time on those famous guidelines which concern our hon. colleagues today.
We find that the first of these guidelines, which deals with local administration, that far from depriving band councils of powers, it seeks to codify existing powers and even add new ones. For instance, guideline No. 1 provides that budgetary planning for all the needs of the local community, namely general budgeting, should be approved by the band council.
Moreover, these guidelines provide that the council is accountable for the financial administration to every band member and is also accountable to the funding agencies mostly to the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
The guideline still grants the band council the right to hire qualified personnel, to supervise the conduct of the band members, to make sure they abide by the guidelines, to investigate and to institute proceedings if necessary and to take disciplinary action against those who refuse to obey. It might be added that any band member can ask to examine the minutes of the band council.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, this first guideline, is merely a codification of what already existed, and its 14 headings are all related to the processes of such a financial management. And after having read and reread in Shakespeare's language, this first guideline, I did not find anything, Mr. Speaker, which might lead one to conclude that the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development wants to impose in a paternalistic way on the bands or on the Indian councils some things they do not want to hear about.
The second guideline applies to district councils. Two months ago, while visiting some parts of my riding of Charlevoix, I had the opportunity to discuss with the band council of one of the reservations, in Les Escoumins, and with another, in Bersimis, two Montagnais reservations. In both cases, I was asked to study the possibilities for them to set up a district council. In an area where, for instance, a distance of 1,000 miles separates the Montagnais on the North Shore from the neighbouring reservation, a district council is of prime importance. I am sure that the second guideline which deals with the district councils will, in the main, meet the demands I have received from the Indians in my area.
This district council is created at the request of the bands, which in turn become members of the council. There again, Mr. Speaker, I am quite sure that is not an ex cathedra requirement on the part of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. The council is answerable to the band members; there is therefore double protection. The band councils are responsible for the creation of the district council which in turn is answerable to the band members.
Each band must have at least one representative on the district council, and the band itself designates its representative. The band leaders can and may join or leave the
June 12, 1975

district council at will. They must, however, consult the band members before doing so, and also vote on a resolution of the band council to either join or leave the district council.
A band council which is a member of a district council can manage its own programs at the local level, or ask the district council to manage it on its behalf. There again, the band councils are not being forced to give up any of their present powers. To my mind, the guidelines on the district council have been welcomed by the majority of band councils at the local level. The district council will be financed. It will include in its budget all the responsibilities which fall to a council of that type, for example the salaries of employees, the rental of premises, travels from one band to another or to meetings, as well as the profes-sionnal assistance they may need to get information or to learn the best ways to appeal either to the department or to other finance organizations.
Then, the bands will participate directly in the financing of the district council by contributing to its administration 4 per cent of their basic budget for the first year, then 8 per cent and finally 16 per cent. For its part, in the first three years, the department will help to solve the problems the district councils may experience at the beginning.
The other guidelines deal with the basic financing of bands. It is useless to go into details, except to say that so many dollars are given for each Indian or Eskimo. The other guideline, the fourth one, is about program funding. I will not go into details here either.
But there is still one thing I want to mention. In the last eight years, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has been perhaps the most aware of the wishes of the native population compared to other departments with other segments of the Canadian population.
The fact that we listened attentively to the band councils and to the Indian population in general enables us today to be proud when we meet our native people to tell them about all our assistance program to industry, for example about all the programs we have to give them better municipal facilities, or a better education, because it is true that all-
If the hon. member has a question, maybe he could ask it.
The statistics quoted this afternoon by some of my colleagues to prove that the native people do not have their fair share of the Canadian wellbeing, that the young people in Indian reserves are the less educated of all young Canadians, and that health and education services there are the worst, are true, and the Minister of Indian Affairs is extremely aware of it, as his officials are, but we cannot-

speechtext:
All right. The bands in my constituency have made no representations to me criticizing the guidelines issued by the department. As the minister said at the beginning of his speech, he himself has on hand enough supporting texts and evidence to show that some Indian organizations in Canada agree with his guidelines.
I agree with the hon. members opposite who said, before I was interrupted, that the native people's problems were much more critical than the white people's. We are aware of those problems. It is during the much more serene discussions we can have in the Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development that we shall be able to find solutions to the problems of these people, who have the right to demand that the Canadian Parliament administer their affairs more efficiently, and also that we give them more power, because they are entitled to it.
I think that the current review of the legislation on Indian affairs is providing all Indian organizations and bands of Canada with the opportunity to participate in formulating legislation which will allow them to live on the same level as all other Canadians. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the short time that I have I intend to document some of the many problems of native people and then to agree with some of the philosophies that the minister and his staff have put forward. I think they are commendable and are some we should be practising with native people. I intend to go on from that point to disagree with the methods, and to demonstrate that those methods in fact will change those philosophies because they are actually in contradiction one with the other. I will do that by a direct analysis of some of the clauses included in program circular D-l. There can be no doubt about the number of extreme problems that face native people as they face other people.
The preceding speaker mentioned that the Department of Indian Affairs has been most receptive to the needs of the native people. I challenge that. If that is so, how come in 1973 the national average for unemployment of Indians was 56 per cent, and during the winter months was as high as 80 per cent? How come the Indian Association of Alberta estimated that of the 4,445 employable reserve Indians in northern Alberta, only 236 had jobs? That represents a 94 per cent unemployment rate.
29576-11 Vi

June 12, 1975
Indian Affairs
I ask members opposite how come the annual average per capita income registered for Indian people is only $500 as compared to Prince Edward Island, which has the lowest per capita income of any province in Canada, with $2,188? I ask those members who think everything is O.K. in the Indian situation today how come there is a need for 10,000 new homes and 5,000 major repair jobs on existing homes, as well as 5,000 more homes that will be needed over the next five years? These figures are very large when we consider there are only 60,000 four-person Indian families in Canada.
The occupancy average in this country is 3.7 people per 5.3 rooms. However, on Indian reservations the occupancy rate is 6.4 persons in 3.6 rooms. It is rather interesting to note that in patting themselves on the back the Department of Indian Affairs have not told the whole story. I simply look at the 1972-73 annual report. Therein it was mentioned that while the Canadian public had 98 per cent electricity in their homes, native people had 79 per cent electricity. That is a pretty high statistic and it looks pretty good.
Why is it the department did not say these things? Why did they not tell us that while 97 per cent of Canadians generally had running water, only 31 per cent of the native people had running water? While 96.1 per cent of the Canadian people had indoor toilets, only 24 per cent of the native people had them. While 93 per cent had indoor baths, only 19 per cent of native people had indoor baths.
Quite clearly all is not well on the reservations. I think the more devastating statistics deal with life itself. How come in Canada, one of the richest nations in the world, the infant mortality rate is 20 people per 1,000 live births on the national average and yet we are willing to accept 40 deaths per 1,000 for registered Indians, and 70 for Innuits? How can we justify, in a country like Canada, Indian people having a life expectancy of only 36 years and Innuits only 20, when the population at large enjoys a life expectancy of 62 years?
I could go on with considerable data to demonstrate that in the fields of education, crime, and many other areas there are in fact large problems. However, it is not those problems we want to dwell on today. The motion before us deals specifically with program circular D-l which, while I claim it has the right philosophy, has established a set of methods that in fact make it totally unworkable.
To move toward that point I want to share from the field of social science perhaps one of the greatest psychologists this world has witnessed, Erick Erickson, who talked about the importance of autonomy. I think the minister recognizes that, but he does not recognize how it is arrived at. He told about giving the Indian people autonomy. In his speech earlier today he said the fact of the matter is autonomy is not a thing you give, it is a human characteristic that is developed by being allowed to practice certain kinds of behaviours.
When we do an analysis of program circular D-l we find there is no allowance for autonomy. It dictates what one must do. It does not provide for the kind of inward soulsearching and incentive that lead to autonomy, as that word is used in the field of psychology. I refer to behavioural psychologist B. F. Skinner who claims that "the need to be positively reinforced by recognizing and having a

sense of self-worth is essential to developing a constructive individual". Program circular D-l is absolutely in opposition to those principles.
Professor Jack Gibb wrote, and his title is most descriptive, "Is Help Helpful?". He states that when we help people, what we are often trying to do is free them or release them. Yet the very nature of help is often just the opposite. Instead of freeing people it creates a greater dependency. Instead of releasing them, it increases the need and locks them in. I cite as an example of this the statement of the welfare people in the state of New York. It clearly demonstrated that the people in that state had greater difficulty getting off welfare than getting on it.
I do not intend or desire to imply a destructive motive or intent on the part of the minister or his department. But, motive aside, program circular D-l is dead wrong. It does things to the Indian people that box them in. It destroys economy and does not allow for the freedom of thinking.
I would like at this time to go into program circular D-l in an attempt to demonstrate that this not only contravenes the Indian Act, but dictates to people in such a way that they have no freedoms. I might just take one example. I will quote clause 4.6 of program circular D-l:
Bands and Innuit settlements have an obligation to contribute towards the cost of local government according to their resources and ability to pay. It is expected that this principle will apply to core funding as circumstances permit.
This clause may well force the bands to use bands funds for administration and delivery of services. That is a responsibility that was guaranteed by the federal government under the Indian Act. What this really means is a changing away from what was written in that act. While that was important, the next clause was even more important. That is 1.2. The definitions (c) and (h) could undermine the powers of the elected chief and council. I quote the last sentence, "and the concurrence of the majority of those present at a meeting obtained".
This could present the opportunity for the chief and council to be outvoted by the band members on any community program. It is not my belief this was the intended meaning. The fact of the matter is that within program circular D-l there are statements which permit local groups in the Indian band to have powers equal to and above those of the chief and council. If that is not a threat to local autonomy there is certainly misunderstanding of what native behaviour has been as long as the Department of Indian Affairs has been relating to it.
The principal issue in this debate is the right of free choice versus government control. We are here today to talk about autonomy and free choice. I should like at this time to share some other concepts that are included in circular D-l. I am quoting from page four, section (e):
No later than the 15th day of each month, prepare and deliver to the council and the department a statement showing:
1.	Itemized receipts and disbursements during the preceding month
2.	Standing of the general ledger balances as of the last day of the preceding month
3.	Standing of all appropriation accounts as at the last day of the preceding month
June 12, 1975

Those are the normal requests one might make when dealing with a household kind of operation. But surely the department recognizes that some of these bands are dealing with millions of dollars. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) doesn't expect people paying taxes to account for millions of dollars within 15 days of the year end. It is folly to demand on the 15th day of every month a full accounting of millions of dollars as some of these bands are now handling, both in government funds and their own funds. That is an unworkable situation.
I quote again one of the Indian people we met in Edmonton recently. He said, "If what the government wants is for us to run a good business, we have no argument. But to impose this on us is an absolute insult."
I should like to read from page five, in clause (f):
At least once weekly deposit all the monies of the band in accordance with these conditions and withdraw the same only in accordance with these conditions.
Again this does not take the situation into account. Some of these people live hundreds and hundreds of miles away from banks. How do you make deposits in and withdrawals when the bank isn't there? Does the department propose to build banks in every little Indian settlement all through the north country? This is the kind of insensitivity the department shows.
If we turn to page six under section F dealing with purchasing, in 6.2, we find:
No purchase or expenditure is to be approved nor are funds to be expended or committed for any purpose which is not provided for in the budget and in accordance with these conditions.
Then we turn to section H under Disbursements and in 8.3 we read this line:
A petty cash fund is to be established not to exceed $50-
This means they must budget for everything, but they cannot have more than $50 for petty cash. I simply ask: how are they going to budget for a hurricane or the herd bull dying on an Indian ranch? Does this mean they can only buy a $50 bull? You don't budget for those kinds of things like a home burning down. This is the kind of boxing in no one can claim gives anyone any sense of autonomy. This is a dictate from on high, an erector kit on how to run an Indian reserve. This is the government saying in a pamphlet, "Indian Reserves made easy, step A, step B."
Take a look at 8.6. It reads as follows:
No band cheques are to be postdated or signed in blank.
I ask this question if we are giving so much autonomy to the people. Why not? Why, if they are dealing with certain kinds of bills, those that re-occur monthly, especially when so many of them live far away from their businesses, can cheques not be postdated? Where is the authority by which we assume we have the privilege to tell people how they must behave? This is certainly not what we would do with any other sector of society, and it is not something which ought to happen to native people.
Let me put forward another example, this time under J, section (a):
Where a contract is expected to exceed $100 written tenders are invited.
Indian Affairs
I know the minister says he is going to change this figure from $100 to $500 but that still does not satisfy the situation. I come from a farming, ranching community and I know that the rear tire on a tractor will cost anywhere from $800 to $1600 to repair. I know what it is like in a farm situation when you get into the month of October and you are still combining.
What happens when anyone across Canada who is not Indian has a flat rear tire on his tractor? In harvest season you go in and get it changed and have a new one put on within two or three hours. But what about native people? According to these guidelines they must tender and then wait for five days. That is what the guidelines say. If they have to wait for five days in harvest season when the sun is shining, there is no one here who cannot say this is a regimented, dictated kind of paper which takes any autonomy away from native people, and if they become insulted and react to this, then all I can suggest is that they have every right to become insulted because this is a paper which dictates to them step by step how their lives should be run.
What we have here is a paint-by-numbers Indian program, established in an attempt to make people fit into boxes and categories when in fact people don't fit that way. The Indian people have told us over and over again that if what we are asking for is that they run their financial affairs with good, sound, business practices then, of course, there is no argument. But to impose program circular D.I. on them is an absolute insult.
I think I have some time left in which to speak but I see it is six o'clock. I will therefore call it six o'clock and continue at eight o'clock.

If we turn to page 10 of the program, we read under 10.3:
Travel expenses for all employees are to be paid subject to the submission of an itemized account of claim. Treasury Board regulations may be used as a guide but the rates contained therein are not to be exceeded.
I simply ask: how is that for trust in the promotion of autonomy? What about the special travel conditions of northern communities and why is it there isn't some allowance for the native people to make these decisions themselves?
Then I note on page 11, under the section Audit:
Any official appointed by the department to perform an audit or program review function is to be given full access at reasonable times to the financial and other program records of the band.
May I make this absolutely clear. The program circular D-l requires the native people to secure an audit. We now hear that the department are coming in with their own audit and double checking. We do not do that with other people in society, so we cannot go forward and claim that, this being the case, we are giving our native people some autonomy, some opportunity for self-direction.

June 12, 1975
Indian Affairs
In the few moments I have left I want to say that nothing could be more correct than to extend to our native people a sense of self-government, to give them a feeling of pride, a feeling that they are people who can work and manage their own affairs.
I think we have had enough experience by this date in our history to recognize that what we are dealing with is behaviour. Behaviour is not a thing that is changed by a dictate from above; behaviour is changed by allowing people opportunity and by extending to them trust. We cannot do that by a regimented, boxed-in set of regulations which simply concludes that all native people are in the same situation, wherever they exist in whatever part of Canada.
If we are going to have program guidelines, then I think they need to be of a broad, general, and philosophical form, leaving the flexibility to the native people, even if the minister wishes to seek their stamp of approval. But the native Indian people need to be able to say: "These guidelines match your philosophy". If they put forward these guidelines and the minister can accept them, I think we need not turn out a heavy, weighty book, that goes from coast to coast and from the 49th parallel to the north pole, one that assumes that native people are all in the same condition and prescribes to them how they should account for all funds. These people are unique, they are individual, and they are human beings. I agree with the philosophy and I hope that the methods can be changed to permit this to take place.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am happy to be able to join in this debate tonight. We have heard quite a few contributions, some of which contained some positive points, but I am a bit disturbed by some of the negativism we have heard today.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext: Constructive criticism.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext:
Yes, some of it was, I must agree.
Having regard to these guidelines, I must say that locally administered programs are quite common to most Canadians. They are, indeed, the backbone of our way of self-government. To Indian communities, most of which are publicly financed, locally administered programs are but 10 years old. It is now just 10 years since the government began to provide funds to Indian bands so they could administer programs which, up to that time, had been entirely in the hands of federal civil servants. In that time the local government program has made an enormous contribution to the self-reliance of the Indian community. Band administration has grown and developed rapidly.

As the minister has said many times, we are encouraged by the increasing number of bands that have assumed program responsibilities. It reflects an increasing awareness by the Indian people, and a move away from dependency upon the government. Their initiative has substituted a greater and more positive measure of self-reliance, and we should all continue to do whatever we can to encourage and, indeed, foster, this move toward
self-responsibility.
Indian band administrations will manage over $100 million in this fiscal year. Consider these facts: 510 bands administer one or more programs; 425 bands employ a total of 2,600 persons on band staff, and 132 bands will administer in excess of $200,000 per band in this fiscal year.
There have been criticisms of this program during this debate, some of which have been harsh. I think some of the things that have been said have been misguided, but I am happy to say there has been no general feeling expressed that Indian people cannot or should not manage programs. No one has said that.
Ten years ago there were those who predicted failure, but they have been proven wrong. The late Arthur Laing, when he was the minister, said that he expected some bands would make mistakes. He said that was acceptable to a degree, because mistakes are the best way of learning. In many respects I am pleased that it is the mistakes of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development that preoccupy this House, for it could have been quite different.
But that faith was not misplaced. Indian bands in general have done an excellent job. They have reason to be proud, and it is pride that has led to much of the complaining about the guidelines. It is not that they are offensive to the Indian tribes; not at all, but they have been taken to be offensive.
What do these guidelines reflect? They put forward a proposed set of operating rules so that band administrators know what is expected of them. Where bands already have such rules there is no problem. It becomes merely a matter of indicating that their rules are as good or better than the guidelines issued by the department. In this case their own manual of procedure will apply.
These guidelines are simply and straightforwardly a set of rules to ensure that public funds-substantial amounts of public funds-are spent in a sensible and proper manner. They are for the protection of the Indian administrators and the public purse. I am sure members of the opposition would be very quick to criticize the government if it authorized the expenditure of these sums of moneys without any control on how they are spent.
Without guidelines unfair criticism can be based on nothing but a whim of the critic. We have seen an indication of that in the debate today. With general rules laid down, the band administration has a perfect defence; that is, that the rules were observed. As the trade union people say, a good, workable, collective agreement is the foundation for a good, working relationship. I think few will argue that there is no need for rules. The public funds of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development must be accountable in the same way other money

voted by parliament for other government departments is accountable. I have not heard anyone here advocate the abolition of the Auditor General or Treasury Board, or repeal of the Financial Administration Act.
There are four main charges brought against the guidelines. First, they are said to have been developed without consultation; second, they are said to jeopardize local government in Indian communities; third, they are said to be a step toward what is called the white paper policy; fourth, they are said to infringe on Indian freedom, threaten cultural identity, and damage the relationship between the department and the Indian people.
