speechtext:
I thank hon. members for their applause. I hope they will continue to listen as attentively as they have because they will probably learn more.
There was consultation. The consultation demonstrated the need for rules and guidelines. At 28 meetings held in many different parts of Canada the Indian people-band administrators, chiefs, and councillors-told the staff of Indian Affairs that a manual of local government was needed. They said it was vital they be told what was expected of them. They complained about lack of standardized rules and procedures under which they could operate. They said they were subjected to unfair criticism because they did not do what was wanted. They went on to say no one told them exactly what it was that was wanted.
The need was plainly and clearly there for guidelines. It was then decided to put forward some guidelines for discussion and for testing in practice. The education guidelines, for example, were developed in close consultation with the National Indian Brotherhood, its affiliated organizations, chiefs, and councils. They were discussed at length at many stages of their development.
The guidelines were then presented to the executive committee of the NIB. Their reaction was that they wanted no guidelines. That is all very well, but it is not consultation. When the department is told that the Indian people want to know where they stand and then brings forward guidelines so the Indian people will know where they stand, the taxpayer is entitled to a great deal more than that response. The department has consulted the Indian people and is prepared to adapt and adjust its proposals to meet any realistic suggestions for improvement. The guidelines suggest that changes be put forward. Where a band has a better way or an equivalent way, the department is prepared to accept it.
Earlier in the debate the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) said that he hoped the minister would take the opportunity to set straight a few things he mentioned this afternoon. I think it might be a good idea if the same hon. member would be a little more careful in respect of some of the things he puts forward. For example, he said in his speech that regional directors of the Indian Affairs branch were instructed that the
Indian Affairs
guidelines were to be put in place by the end of June, 1975, or funds would be cut off. That is not so.
I should like to quote from a directive from the Assistant Deputy Minister of Indian and Eskimo Affairs to the regional directors. It states as follows:
It would appear that in some regions, bands are being told that unless they produce a BCR adopting the D-l verbatim, funds will be cut off July 1, 1975. This is not the interpretation to be given to my earlier instructions because bands are free to establish their own rules and regulations provided they embody the principles listed earlier and are consistent with the intent of the various requirements contained in D-l.
While the circulars (guidelines) which have been issued will remain in effect, they are to be treated as being of an interim character pending consideration of changes proposed by the Indian people.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that is a process of consultation. Why were the guidelines issued? There are three very cogent reasons. One would be to protect the band chiefs and councillors from undue criticism from band members. The second would be to safeguard the use of public funds, and the third would be to extend to members of the bands the right to know how the funds are being spent. Instead of being an infringement of freedom in relation to the native peoples I submit that the guidelines will become a guarantee of freedom.
Now I should like to refer to the second point I mentioned. The guidelines do not jeopardize or threaten the structure of local government. They strengthen and enhance it. They reinforce the authority, responsibility and accountability of chiefs and councils. They are far less onerous or restrictive than those imposed by provinces upon municipalities. They are the minimum controls the public is entitled to expect. Not only that, but almost all bands operating programs are already meeting the requirements. These guidelines simply specify the terms and conditions under which public funds are turned over to Indian bands to manage. Far from being a step toward some fancied goal of assimilation, they are a safeguard that Indian communities can retain local government institutions and operate them within limits that are an inescapable element of personal autonomy and local self-reliance.
The third point is that the guidelines of course have nothing to do with the white paper proposals put forward six years ago. There is not and could not be any connection. The government withdrew the proposals of 1969 and is still awaiting the proposals of the Indians concerning what should be put forward in their place. These guidelines do not portend any amendments to the Indian Act. They do not conceal any deep laid plan to subvert the Indian aspirations. They seek to provide a means for Indian people to achieve the important goal of self-reliance.
The fourth point is that far from infringing or threatening cultural identity they are a recognition of the fact that freedom requires an orderly and lawful setting in which to thrive. It is not, or would not be, freedom to operate without rules. That would be an invitation to some future administration probably to decree that the experiment of contributions to bands, the turning over of program responsibility, was a failure and must go. Such a judgment might be based on the isolated experience of a few bands. The guidelines are put forward to enable safe, solid and

June 12, 1975
Indian Affairs
sound band administration to grow and prosper while at the same time fulfilling the requirements of parliament in the accountability of public funds. Members may seek the roots for all this in the past, and those disposed to do so will find them. All I am saying is that hon. members and those involved must look to the present and to the future.
For the moment I ask members of the House to consider some of their own responsibilities to the public, to the rules they have themselves laid down, such as the Financial Administration Act and others, and then to ask themselves how they can advocate the transfer of in excess of $100 million to individuals and groups without rules.
Having said these things, Mr. Speaker, let me hasten to add that the guidelines were a first proposal put forward in good faith to provide the basis for a future set of rules upon which hopefully everyone can agree. Let me repeat what the minister has said.

And

The guidelines are necessary, Mr. Speaker, and I am surprised to find them characterized as they have been.
The guidelines have been developed to support seven basic principles: first, that the Indian community itself- those who elect the chief and council, be informed and support the concept of band administration of programs and especially such vital community programs as economic development and education; second, that band administration will require qualified staff to provide a proper level of service to the community; third, that public funds provided to bands must be used for the purpose for which they are intended and must be properly accounted for just as are other public funds; fourth, that individual rights be protected-band members have a right to be fully informed of the total sums received by the band and of how these funds have been spent; fifth, inventories and records of band assets are to be kept to ensure that those things purchased on behalf of all do not become the private possessions of the few; sixth, that band methods of purchasing supplies and services should conform to sound business and administrative practices; seventh, that both the bands' and the department's responsibilities should be as clearly defined as possible.
The guidelines were not designed to restrict bands in the management of programs; they are to assist. They provide a sound basis for bands to discuss and negotiate so

that practices which are developed to meet local needs also meet the fundamental need of sound administration.
The department is not ramming these guidelines down anyone's throat and no money is being withheld from anyone because of these guidelines. But I think the Indian community is entitled to accountable institutions of local government, and I know of no other way to ensure they get them than by providing them with funds so they may develop institutions and by making certain they know what they have to do to discharge the functions for which the money is paid.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was beginning to wonder whether we were going to have a new set of guidelines tonight because the hon. member seemed to be enumerating them.
It gives me pleasure to join in the debate because, having been a member of parliament for a few years now,
I find that often we do not have the opportunity to debate the affairs of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and often we find that it is difficult to put forward suggestions from all sides of the House regarding how we should pursue the affairs of the department.	,
Tonight my comments will be almost totally on the issue of consultation, and I would like to start by reading part of a telegram that was sent to me by the Samson band in Hobbema, Alberta. It reads as follows:
Regarding local government guidelines housing policy education it has come to the attention of the chief in council of Samson band that all funding from the Department of Indian Affairs will be cut off if the bands do not accept the guidelines as set out by the Department of Indian Affairs. We wish to emphasize that there was no consultation with the chiefs and councils prior to the implementation date of April 1, 1975.
I must point out that at the time of receipt of this telegram I had not even laid eyes on the guidelines. It strikes me that the minister has handled the issue of these guidelines and circulars in an extremely unsatisfactory manner. The program circulars seemed to be simply thrown out of the blue, and members of parliament were not even allowed the courtesy of being provided with guidelines before they were given to the Indian people. I am not saying that they should have but it seems to me that, since we are the representatives of the Indian people in this House of Commons, surely we should have been given these guidelines so that we could have looked at them and dealt with them at the same time as the Indian people.
Another suggestion is that a change of policy such as this should have been put before the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs so that they could have dedicated two or three meetings to this subject, looked at these guidelines, and suggested ways in which they could be improved. But none of this was done.
My personal experience was that I was unable to obtain a copy of these guidelines. I did not even know about them until I went to the Hobbema council meeting on May 20, 1975. I understand that these five guidelines became effective as of April 1, and any Indian bands which did not conform with the provisions set forth in the circulars were not given these guidelines until well into May. I was informed of them on May 20. I note with interest that the
June 12, 1975

copies of the circulars that I now have in my possession were all dated February and March. I would be most anxious to hear the minister justify the two to three months' time lag which existed between February, March and May when these guidelines were finally distributed.
I would also like to emphasize that during my meeting with the 4-Band council I learned that only three copies of these guidelines were circulated to the whole treaty area, which probably consist of well in excess of 10 or 12 bands. In view of the great number of various governmental communiques, departmental pamphlets, and booklets that have crossed my desk in the past three or four months, I would suspect that the distribution of an exceedingly limited number of guideline copies to members of parliament and Indian bands was not caused by a shortage of paper or a malfunctioning of the printing process, but rather by sheer negligence and little regard for the rights of members of parliament on this side of the House and of the Indian people.
The Indian bands maintain that there was a lack of consultation with the chiefs and councils prior to the implementation date of April 1. In 1969, when the white paper on Indian affairs was rejected by the Indian associations and eventually rejected by the government, the Indians were assured that no new policies or directives would be put into effect without detailed negotiations and consultation or without the consent of the Indian people. However, in spite of these commitments, the department has now developed policy circulars without full dialogue or consultation with the Indian people.
The minister stated in the House on May 6, and I quote: "there has been considerable consultation on these guidelines", yet I have before me several communications-of which I have read one-from various bands, all of which state in no uncertain terms that the circulars were not circulated to the bands and councils, and that no consultations were had with the councils.
I must confess that when the minister was questioned about with whom consultation had taken place, he did not say that conferences had been held with various Indian bands but, and again I quote, "with the Indian bands, or the National Indian Brotherhood". I received a telegram from the president of the National Indian Brotherhood to Harold Cardinal, President of the Alberta Indian Association, dated April 29. Admittedly the minister met with the N.I.B. on April 15, but at that time the N.I.B. was urging the freezing of the implementation of these guidelines and program regulations, a request which the minister has obviously refused.
In the aforementioned telegram Mr. Manuel, President of the National Indian Brotherhood, terms the guidelines as objectionable, states that the N.I.B. is unaware of any Indian leaders accepting such policy guidelines and regulations, and emphasizes the importance of Indian involvement in all decisions affecting community programs. My obvious question to the minister is what is his definition of the word "consult"? Is it a matter of consulting with just one band and assuming that all the others agree?
The case in point typifies the position the government has taken vis-a-vis Indians over the course of several
Indian Affairs
years in the matter of consultation. Only last fall a similar situation arose with respect to Bill C-15, the Indian oil and gas bill. I have before me several communications received from Indian bands in which it is maintained that no discussion was held with the Indians prior to the introduction of the bill before the House. I will just read one from the Blood tribe in Alberta:
Request that no legislation be cast regarding Bill C15 until consultation has taken place with the Indians.
Speaking of that particular piece of legislation, on November 28 of last year I rose under the provisions of Standing Order 43 and moved that the money owing to Indian bands from the collection of the export tax on oil extracted from Indian reserves be paid to them to enable them to honour their economic contracts. On the same day a question of mine appeared on the order paper in which I asked the minister when the money would be returned to the bands and whether interest payments would be coming to them in view of the lateness of the return. The minister replied that the matter was under discussion and consultation with the province of Alberta. Several questions have since been asked on this subject, and the minister's response has always been the same.
Only last week I received an answer to questions I posed on November 5 of 1974. My questions were very specific: how much money is presently held in the federal treasury collected from the export tax on oil? Was any money collected after April 1, and does the government intend to return all this money to Indian bands? This question has just been answered, and the answer is that discussions on the substance of this question are being held among a number of departments, and until these discussions are completed and a decision has been reached, no substantive reply can be made.
It seems obvious that the ministers are dragging their heels on this matter, because to date nothing has happened. No two way discussions are presently taking place between the federal and provincial governments. A telephone conversation I had just yesterday with the minister in charge of Indian affairs in Alberta revealed that when the federal minister was out there this was not even on the agenda, and he knew nothing of it. Of course he is a new minister, and I suppose that may be one of the reasons, but if there was continued consultation on a matter as important as this, surely the new minister should be brought up to date because this matter is of concern to the Indian people. My assumption is-and this is a guesstimate-that there may be $2 million, $3 million, $4 million or $5 million sitting around, hopefully in a fund, but perhaps even in the treasury. No interest is being paid on it, and it seems like the federal ministry hopes it will go away because it is certainly not pursuing the matter. As long as I am standing in my place in this House I can assure the minister that I will pursue it.

speechtext:
I wish to comment briefly on one aspect of the guidelines which is of great concern to Indian bands within my riding. No one will dispute the fact that the Indian people should be accountable for their funds. It has been emphasized by all hon. members that there is no argument whatsoever in this regard, but I do
6710

June 12, 1975
Indian Affairs
believe that the exceedingly elaborate accounting system required by the provisions in these new guidelines is totally unreasonable and unnecessary.
Presently it appears extremely difficult for the bands to operate under the provisions of these guidelines. In my riding of Wetaskiwin the bands at Hobbema and Winter-burn have a great deal of funds. These two sets of funds must be co-ordinated within this program. The Indian bands receive their funds through natural gas and oil revenues, royalties, agriculture, horticultural developments and things of this sort, and they are substantial.
Today government funds are accounted for to the government and to the Indian people within the band, and their own funds are accounted for to the people within the band. Revenues obtained from the government under the new system must be accounted for, but because these bands have a large amount of their own funds, the amount given to them by the federal government is somewhat less than that given to other bands. This is all right.
It was pointed out in a question I asked the minister that his program works in much the same manner as the DREE program works; namely, that those bands which are not as wealthy as others receive more federal funding, and I think this is a good program. It should be continued, but when the bands are receiving money from the federal government and using those funds in conjunction with their own funds to buy equipment and to run their every day operations and businesses, how do they account? The only way they can account for these funds under the new guidelines is to hire a chartered accountant and a number of people to back him up. This will amount to an unrealistic expenditure, especially when under their own band administration now they are adequately accounting for all these funds.
I feel that some way has to be worked out so that these restrictive guidelines can be adapted so that they can work in harmony with what is now in effect and with what is now being suggested by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development in its guidelines.
In conclusion, I request that a moratorium be placed on these new guidelines until either the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development refers to these guidelines and amendments are made, or until adequate consultation takes place between the Indian people and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development so that the amendments which the Indian people feel are necessary can be embodied in these guidelines. With that, I hope the minister takes these representations to heart and that he will grant us this moratorium.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, currently more than 500 of the 567 Indian bands across Canada are administering various programs, and over $100 million will go directly to band councils this * year to administer programs on behalf of their members. These are programs like housing, education, social services, etc.
In 1965 the department introduced the contributions to bands program which enabled councils to operate specific

local programs. The move represented the first step toward local government. Because of the positive response of bands and the expanding nature of the program, a departmental task force was formed in late 1972 to chart a course for the future. Councils, associations, conferences and individuals submitted briefs and position papers. All of the recommendations of the Indian people were accepted. Two recommendations in particular, the transfer of capital and operations-maintenance funds, and the setting up of band core funding, were indispensable first steps toward local government. The task force report made the objective clear-all programs that could be managed at the community level should be. The department's obligations, on the other hand, required its involvement to ensure adequate levels of service and to guarantee appropriate use of public funds. The task force recommendations also made clear that there must be general guidelines or regulations for band operations.
The department's push for local government is not a cop-out of its responsibilities. The former minister, who is now President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien), in a letter to the Quebec regional chiefs said:
Local government... will in no way jeopardize the reserve system, nor the status of Indians, nor the funds, services and programs available from the Government of Canada. On the contrary, I firmly believe that local government... is a prerequisite for maintaining your way of life, your identity, your pride, and your opportunity for meaningful participation in Canadian society.
That statement is still departmental policy.

speechtext: Amen.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext:
Amen.
On April 24 the Union of B.C. Indian Chiefs passed a resolution calling upon all Indians in the province to reject, as of May 1, funds from all federal departments and agencies, including the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
The expressed wish of Indians in British Columbia to reduce their dependence on government, to stress self-reliance and to assume substantially greater responsibility for the management of their own affairs, corresponds closely with my own view. The long-term objectives of the government must be to give greater responsibility to the native peoples. The present act gives responsibilities to the minister which cannot be given to the native peoples. For instance, the responsibility for the management of public funds cannot be given to them, since the minister is accountable to the government for these expenditures.
The Indian Affairs budget in British Columbia for the current year is about $61 million. Salaries account for only $10 million; approximately $5 million is paid for salaries for teachers and other education staff. Therefore, approximately $5 million is spent on departmental salaries by the Department of Indian Affairs in British Columbia.
In 1975 band councils were administering approximately $20 million in funds. As I say, the Indian Affairs budget in British Columbia is about $61 million; if one deducts $10 million, of which about half is for salaries of people I mentioned, the balance available is $51 million.
Indian representatives in British Columbia have justly expressed particular concern about the prolonged delays
June 12, 1975

in the negotiation of their land claims. I share their concern, Mr. Speaker, as do many others in British Columbia. Since the Indian interest involves provincial land and resources, the province must be a party to any settlement which is made with the native peoples of British Columbia. Compensation is a matter for negotiation between the federal government and the province of British Columbia. I stress that this long festering problem will not be settled until the provincial government is willing to sit down and negotiate with the federal government. I am glad that the present and previous ministers have made known a number of times their willingness to sit down with the government of British Columbia and negotiate the settlement of this problem which has long festered in British Columbia.
I ask British Columbia in all seriousness and honesty to negotiate with the federal government in good faith, so that a policy can be formulated. The governments could then go the native peoples of British Columbia and sit down and attempt to solve this problem which has existed since British Columbia entered Confederation. Our native peoples have endured great difficulties for almost 100 years, because no treaty had been signed by the B.C. and the Government of Canada. This is not a new question; this is a matter with which provincial governments of the 1870's and 1880's had to grapple. The present government of British Columbia can now rectify a problem which has existed for almost 100 years. I ask the government to shoulder its responsibilities and I would praise it if it were willing to sit down and negotiate the settlement of this problem. That a government elected by the people of British Columbia should want to wash its hands of jurisdictional responsibility for the native peoples of British Columbia I consider criminal.
I commend ministers who said they are willing to settle these longstanding problems. I wish the provincial government would be as far-sighted as Laurier, who said near the turn of the century that we must settle these problems. I hope that when the year 2,000 or 3,000 arrives there will not be people in this country making the pious assertion that, "This is not our responsibility; it is the federal government's responsibility. Please do not bother us with these mundane problems." The problem should be solved. Our native peoples have been long suffering. As some hon. members may know, blockades have taken place in British Columbia. Native peoples have taken over Indian Affairs offices. Although I do not condone lawlessness-

-I sympathize with people whose grievance is long standing. Perhaps the native people of British Columbia have been too forbearing in their attitude; their recent actions in the province have drawn attention to their problems. I warn the native people of British Columbia not to take out their frustrations on innocent bystanders like loggers, who were prevented from earning a living by blockades. Indian Affairs
The Attorney General of British Columbia must enforce the law in British Columbia but, at the same time, it is the responsibility of the two levels of government which could act in this area to sit down together and, with the Indian peoples, start negotiating a settlement. As it is, little or nothing has been done for too many years. We have heard much talk, which is why the native peoples may be correct when they say the white man talks with a forked tongue. We have talked out of one side of our faces, or the other, for many years.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext: Especially the Liberals.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext:
It has been held that, under the act of union, the federal government has the right to ask the province of British Columbia for land for native peoples. Of course we are speaking of provincial land, Crown land. Although the federal government has not written to B.C. saying, "We want this section or that section of land." the federal government position has been that this is provincial land and the province should be brought into the negotiations.
The native peoples have said with justification, "Look, don't talk about land alone; talk about an economic base as well. We need an economic base; we need resources; we want something our people can work on." This is why in negotiations with the province, they have to discuss tree farm licences, for example, with stumpages paid by them the same as anyone else. This will give them an economic base on which to work. There is no point putting them on a reserve and letting them starve to death. I hope governments do not decide to put them some place and keep them on welfare and whatever else we can give them to keep them quiet, hoping they will go away. That would be as wrong as what happened in the past.
There must be some economic base. It must be one on which both the federal and provincial governments cooperate to set it up. The problems which native people have today cannot be solved by talking about alcoholism and drugs, but by giving them an economic base so they can have pride in their way of life and their culture. The first step toward providing this pride is to give them some base on which to develop their reserve life.
Recently members of the standing committee had the privilege of visiting Huron Village outside Quebec City. There are about 1,500 people on that reserve, with six or seven factories which are not run by the government, but by the people of Huron Village. Their problem is not normal to most reserves in Canada. There is a shortage of native people because they are all employed. They are now seeking white people to work there. This is the sort of thing we want to encourage in co-operation with the provincial government. It is also to their benefit to have a strong native industry that is not only a credit to the federal government or the people of Canada but to the people who live in that particular province.
This is why I feel the British Columbia government must enter into negotiations with those in my constituency for the benefit of the native people and the people of British Columbia as well as for the general over all health of Canada.
29576-12Vi

June 12, 1975
Indian Affairs
Pride as a native Canadian can only be achieved when handouts are stopped. I think, for example, of the Duncan area, the Chemainus Indians of Vancouver Island, who have developed a fruit and vegetable co-op which employs the people on reserves. It generates an annual salary of approximately $500,000, and within two years it will probably be up to $1 million. This could be achieved on many of our reserves. We have not given these people money. We have loaned them money which will be repaid by the federal government.
That is one way of solving a problem. It is not political. If any member thinks it is political, he is probably in the wrong House and probably the wrong country. This is a humanitarian question. I point out to the NDP members that the B.C. government is not recognizing the problem. I submit they are playing politics.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext: As I said, this is a humanitarian question, not one of who is right or wrong or who is the most political. It is a gut issue of how to help these people who have been depressed for too long and, I submit, exploited for too long.

speechtext: By the Liberals.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext:
If the hon. member across the way is concerned, I suggest that he contact the premier of that great republic on the west coast and express his concern. Obviously we, as a Liberal government, are having a very difficult time getting through the mountains, forests and oceans to let him know it is time to quit playing games. The problem will not be solved by rhetoric, but by people with a sincere intent to solve the problem sitting down together. This is not something new. It has been going on for a long time.
Guidelines have been discussed today. They are important. However, we may have gone beyond the guideline situation. This question not only involves the native people of British Columbia, but across Canada. When this is discussed I hope there is more response from other provinces than there has been from my native province.
I would welcome any changes made by the province of British Columbia. I would be happy to praise the premier instead of having to say that his attitude at the present time, if not cavalier, is perhaps bordering on criminal negligence.
This is an important question. I hope those members who are laughing today will assume the seriousness that this requires. There has been too much laughing and joking about this-"the poor red man, he is only a drunkard so why should we bother with him?" There are many people in my province, and indeed my constituency, who say we give them too much. I say in all seriousness that we have a chance of giving them respect by giving them something on which they can base their lives. It may be something entirely different from our concept, but it can be something they can live with and build upon. I hope that it comes in the not too distant future.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity of participating in this debate. I do so with considerable apprehension. I perceive

there to be a deterioration in the relationship between our native people and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I am sorry that is the reason I must participate in this debate.
I have had an opportunity to meet the minister. He is extremely personable and commands respect in this House. However, on the basis of my experience and representations that have been made both in this House and to me from Saskatchewan Indian leaders, including Indian people on the great Beardy reserve whom I have the honour of representing in this House, I am deeply concerned. These people are naturally interested in the problems of Indians today.
I am pleased to note that Chief Standing is in the gallery. He is chief of the Wahpeton band.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext:
He has taken the time and trouble to come here to hear this debate and observe how we in this House of Commons deal with affairs related to Indians. There is great concern, and this is why Chief Standing is here. The chief is a member of the Federation of Saskatchewan Indians. He has met with me and other members of our caucus to discuss the concerns of the Indian people in Saskatchewan today.
I am participating in this debate because I think the Saskatchewan point of view has to be stated. During the past weeks there has been anxious activity by the Indian leaders in my province. It has been directed toward attempts to arrive at serious negotiations with the department.
In the course of their efforts in this regard the Indian leaders made numerous approaches to the minister, the department, and members of parliament from my province, as well as to leaders of each of the political parties in Saskatchewan. I am glad to report that again includes the Progressive Conservatives with their terrific showing in yesterday's election.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext:
As far as I can determine, these Indian leaders have received sympathetic support from each party they have spoken to, with the exception of, unfortunately, the minister and the department. They received a sympathetic hearing from the political leaders in Saskatchewan. I believe the Liberal leader in Saskatchewan even went as far as saying he would personally lead a delegation of Saskatchewan Indians to Ottawa and make representations on their behalf with regard to the position relating to the guidelines being discussed today.
I want to say at the outset that the Indian leaders with whom I have spoken do not for one instant object to the principle of accountability with respect to public moneys received by them. They are in fact anxious to have the expenditure of these funds controlled in ways in which there can be no question about their proper application. I know they feel that it is in the interests of Indian people that there be no question concerning the spending of
June 12, 1975

public moneys, and that any abuses in this area tend to interfere with the advancement they wish for their people.
The question of accountability therefore is not an issue at all in this debate. Rather, the issues that have given rise to this debate are those relating to the government's policies as to the advancement of Indian peoples in our country, and the government's sincerity with respect to developing a policy of self-reliance for our Indian peoples.
I will not take the time of the House to recount the history of the government's handling of Indian affairs over the past years which is known to hon. members and which, unfortunately, manifests itself in the unsatisfactory circumstances of the Indian people today. Suffice it to say that the history of government dealings with Indian people has been exemplified by an attitude of parternal-ism which has thwarted rather than enhanced any aspirations for self-reliance.
Times change, and policies must change in order to adapt to present circumstances. The reserve in the eyes of most Indian leaders has taken on a different complexion in recent years. No longer is it possible for Indian people to look to the reserve as a self-contained, economically self-sufficient unit on which they may remain isolated from the outside world and technological developments. The simple fact of the matter is that the reserve is no longer capable of supporting the Indian peoples and therefore a new role for reserves must be developed and promoted by the department.
I believe the Indian peoples now perceive the reserves as serving two functions. The first function is that of a training ground for their peoples to equip them with basic education, training, and talents to allow them to move off the reserves and into society in our country, and to enter the work force or to compete in the marketplace. In this connection the reserves provide the basic educational and social facility in which Indian peoples may receive instruction, training, and a feeling for their own proud culture, in addition to those standard basic skills obtainable through educational institutions in other parts of the country.
A second function or role of the reserve is to serve as a sort of home to which Indian peoples may return from time to time to be among their own people and unique culture. As a part of the whole process of this development it is imperative that the department create the proper type of motivation and atmosphere conducive to the establishment of self-reliance among the Indian peoples. It is this objective which the government has failed to achieve and which is apparently causing such concern among Indian leaders today.
It is not as if the minister has not received sufficient representation on the concerns of the Indian leaders. The minister is new to his position and I believe that the Indian peoples have been prepared to allow him a reasonable period of time in which to get to know his job. It is not as if, however, the minister had no previous experience with Indian affairs. I understand that he, before his elevation to cabinet, spent some time as chairman of the Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development, and that during this period he spent considerable time studying Indian conditions, attitudes and aspirations. It is therefore surprising and distressing to see that the minis-
Indian Affairs
ter now appears determined to get himself into a position of confrontation with the Indian leaders in our country. A person serving in this portfolio must gain the respect of Indian peoples if he or she hopes to make any progress. The respect of Indian peoples is not obtained by protracted demonstrations of inflexibility.
One appreciates the fact that the minister is in receipt of advice from departmental officials. These departmental officials have apparently devised a system of guidelines which they believe to be appropriate to the circumstances on reserves today. But I would remind the minister that his role is not only to administer his department but to interpret the needs and aspirations of the Indian people. The role of the department is to serve the Indian people- it is not the role of the Indian people to serve the administration.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext:
I personally became cognizant of the implementation of the departmental guidelines in April of this year. Representatives of the Federation of Saskatchewan Indians met with me in my constituency office to say that changes were taking place in the administration of Indian affairs within the province, and guidelines being established without consultation with Indian leaders.
They were concerned about these developments because they said they believed the government when it said that the development of policies relating to Indians would be done only after consultations with the Indian peoples so that such policies would adequately reflect the needs and aspirations of Indians.
They indicated to me that the appointment of Jim Wright as regional director of the department in Saskatchewan, and the arbitrary implementation of the guidelines with respect to education and housing, represented an undermining of the concept of consultation, and that the guidelines further tended to undermine traditional Indian government as reflected in the Indian Act.
The concerns of the Federation of Saskatchewan Indians were relayed to the minister in a question asked in the House by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) on May 6, 1975. At that time the minister was asked about the guidelines. The minister only replied that there had been consultation, but on further questioning by the right hon. member for Prince Albert the minister clearly indicated that, if the guidelines created difficulties and problems, he was prepared to change them.
Since the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert first brought the question of the implementation of guidelines before this House, there have been subsequent and numerous questions and motions relating to the same topic. There has been a plethora of representations and communications from representatives of Indian leaders from across Canada as well as from the National Indian Brotherhood.
Notwithstanding the minister's initial undertaking in response to the question by the right hon. member for Prince Albert on May 6, it has appeared that the minister has become inflexible in his attitude rather than more receptive to the concept of discussion and consultation over the very great concerns expressed by Indian leaders.

June 12, 1975
Indian Affairs

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext: Just like his predecessor.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext:
I have had no opportunity to observe that closer at hand than you, sir, but I accept your advice in that regard. This attitude is exemplified by the fact that since April of this year, notwithstanding what was said by my hon. friend from Northumberland-Miramichi, there has been specific advice given to the bands that unless the guidelines are followed without exception, funding will be terminated as of July 1, 1975.
There must be some written communication to this effect from the departmental officials directed to the bands in the province of Saskatchewan, notwithstanding what directives have come from other parts. But these directives from the minister, or whatever form it is they take, have simply not been related to the bands themselves and they are under great apprehension concerning the termination of funds.
I should like to refer to a letter written to the minister to which was attached any number of vouchers indicating that the funding has been withheld pending passage of the appropriate resolution by the bands in the province of Saskatchewan. The hon. member asked for some proof. I think the attitude of the Saskatchewan chiefs, in light of this situation, has been exemplified by this letter sent to the minister by a distinguished Saskatchewan chief, Sol Sanderson of the James Smith Band at Kinistino, Saskatchewan. Chief Sanderson has written to the minister as of June 9, 1975, as follows, and I want to read this letter into the record because I think it states very well the attitude of Saskatchewan Indians:
The James Smith Band Council will not accept the local government guidelines in spite of the coercion and intimidation tactics used by your acting regional director, Jim Wright.
Mr. Wright has informed us that funding will be cut off July 1 if the guidelines are not accepted.
Enclosed are several fiscal vouchers used by the department, requesting our Band Council Resolutions, accepting the D-l series.
The D-l local government guidelines redefine the authority outside the jurisdiction of the Indian Act. It further gives the local government authority and its chairman the same authority as the chief and council.
There can be no acceptance of this kind of system regardless of the consequences.
Mr. Wm. Dack, the acting district supervisor for Indian affairs in Saskatoon, has stated that all services to our band have been terminated unless we accept Mr. J. Wright and the guidelines.
Funds have been frozen for all band projects and new programs. We do receive some program funds, released at the discretion of the acting regional director. We have not even seen our O. and M. budget for 1975-76. There are no capital projects started in housing or road construction. Our leases are not acted upon by your staff, causing loss of revenue. We are being forced because of this unilateral action by your senior staff to lay off 85 staff members and others are working voluntarily. Several have left the province for employment in the sugar beet fields, rather than return to welfare. The James Smith Band is concerned that you, Mr. Minister, who has demonstrated by your action in Calgary that you do not support sit-ins, has now become part of the movement and you are using the same tactics to achieve your ends by allowing the acting regional director to stage a legal sit-in by terminating services. This is a form of intimidation to force the James Smith Band into submission.
As the Band Council, we documented our concerns and recommendations for administration and we have yet to receive your reply.
We appreciate the concerns you have for accounting of funds. However, we do feel just as strongly about these matters, and we have

presented a proposal for administration and we are presently developing an accounting and recording system with Price-Waterhouse.
The programs and projects developed on our reserve from funding provided by the Department of Indian Affairs has created a strong sense of pride of self-determination. We will not move to militancy to resolve this crisis and we implore upon you to use your office to take immediate action to resolve this crisis.
Our Band Council once again are requesting a meeting with you to discuss the items listed in our previous letter.
That letter, as I have stated, clearly sets out the position and attitude of Saskatchewan Indians today. It is an example of the frustration and concern that they are experiencing. The guidelines of the Indian affairs department are considered by the Indian people as another example of the continuing paternalistic attitude of the government. This attitude is one that tends to manipulate the Indian people. They feel as though they are receiving a series of grants with numerous strings attached, and reams of bureaucratic regulations that restrict the local government's ability to establish its own priorities or to deal with glaring and specific problems of a local nature.
Some chiefs feel that the Indian affairs department is attempting to leave the impression with the general public that the Indians are running around with a pile of the department's money with no strings attached. Nothing could be further from the truth. I believe they are sincerely interested in achieving some form of reasonable control, but that control must be developed through mutual consultation between the minister and his departmental officials and the Indians themselves.
The solution of the government appears to be the creation of guidelines which will make it imperative that outside accounting assistance will be required. The guidelines, as stated, tend to thwart rather than encourage the development of self-reliant skills by the Indian people and are regarded by many as being like killing a fly with a sledgehammer. A guideline that insists upon a precise budget of 10 per cent for office management and 20 per cent for full or part time council staff is not a guideline; it is an imposed instruction, and by its arbitrary nature it interferes with self-government.
Program circular D-l imposes the establishment of a local government authority with equal status to that of the band council. This is interpreted by the Indian people as a total rejection of traditional Indian government, a total usurpation of the powers of the chief and his council, and a policy designed to divide and rule. They consider the imposition of a district council as yet another bureaucracy which can freely walk on to a reserve or have or call a referendum or vote over the heads of the band council and its chief.
In conclusion, Madam Speaker, the Federation of Saskatchewan Indians I sincerely believe has been consistently law abiding, as demonstrated by the letter to which I have just referred. They have been reasonable in their representations. I am concerned that the consultation of which they speak has not taken place. The concept of consultation with the government is not that which the Indian people feel they should receive. If the minister continues his present attitude of inflexibility in respect to this problem I fear that he will have the dubious distinction of presiding over the disintegration of the relation-
June 12, 1975

ship between the Indian people and the government of Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have heard a lot about consultation in this debate. The word has floated over from the government side of the House as members tell us how much the government has consulted the Indian people. Let me tell the House that a few minutes ago the minister was sitting beside my colleague, the hon. member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth), and that was the first meaningful consultation with the Canadian people that I have seen him have since he became minister.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext: He just said "Good evening".

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext:
The hon. member says that even that consultation with the minister just consisted of saying "Good evening" to him. The other thing I have observed while listening to government members making their little set speeches on the motion before the House relates to their use of language when referring to the Indian people. They keep saying things like "We want to protect the bands". They tell us how much they have given them, how much the government has done for them over the last 100 years. This smacks of paternalism, which is the word that they criticized, and said should not be in the motion. This is the most hypocritical group I have seen since I came from colonialist imperial Guyana.
Whether he admits it or not, the minister has a very serious problem of communication. He is going forward willy-nilly with this set of guidelines and he is saying he has consulted. I have here a summary from the National Indian Brotherhood which goes across the country and gives the reactions of the Indian people to his guidelines.
For example, the National Indian Brotherhood itself rejects the guidelines. The Union of B.C. Indian Chiefs opposes any government funds under the present terms of reference. The Indian Association of Alberta has asked until September to review the new guidelines and make the desired changes. The Federation of Saskatchewan Indians has rejected the new guidelines. The Manitoba Indian Brotherhood has rejected the guidelines, and a great majority of the chiefs in Ontario have rejected the guidelines. The Quebec Indian Association is not operating under the new guidelines but under guidelines jointly developed by them and the Department of Indian Affairs. The United New Brunswick Indians have rejected the guidelines, and the United Nova Scotia Indians have rejected them. Whether those on the government benches want to admit it or not, there is a problem. They cannot stick their heads in the sand like an ostrich and hope it will go away.
Having lived under imperialist rule for 18 years I recognize colonialism when I see it. When we were against the masters, using the moneys which were given us by them, and using the system they had, immediately the rules were changed. The rules of the game were changed because we were starting to use the imperialist rules and were making some headway in respect of independence.
Indian Affairs
Here we see this again. As soon as the Indian people start using the wherewithal that was provided by the masters of this political system, and as soon as they know how the system works and start using it to their advantage, then the government immediately changes the rules to keep them off balance. That is colonialism, whether you want to recognize it or not, my friend.
Last August a British organization known as the Minority Rights Group published a report on Canada's native peoples. In this report we find a conclusion which has a bearing on the motion that is before the House today. It states:
The characteristic which every generation and every kind of white policy maker has shared is a capacity for imposing solutions to the "Indian problem" without either consulting or seeking a deep understanding of the Indian himself. Because of this lack of humility they have consistently acted on their own ill-informed and doctrinaire prejudices-
This characteristic can be summed up in two words "colonial paternalism". Although the style of those connected with Indian administration in Canada has changed over the last 100 years, there is little to suggest that the new style has been matched with actions. Since 1968 the Liberal government has been long on rhetoric but short on measures that facilitate an ending to the historic pattern of colonial domination of the Canadian native peoples by the Indian affairs branch. The native peoples know intimately that the new style adopted by the Trudeau government has not led to any transformation in their way of life in the last seven years.
I assure this House that I do not make these charges lightly but only after carefully reviewing the events that led to the policy directives which we are discussing today becoming an issue of national importance.
On May 20 the minister assured us that he was seeking the agreement of bands across Canada for these guidelines that are euphemistically called local government guidelines. Yet these guidelines took effect on April 1, nearly two months before this statement in the House.
I know, for example, that yesterday the minister sent officials to the Yukon to discuss the guidelines with the Yukon Brotherhood. As far as the brotherhood is concerned, this will be the first meaningful discussion of the substance and form of these guidelines to which they have been a party. This is some method of consultation. On May 21 the minister assured this House there had already been consultations on these guidelines. The minister's definition of "consultation" appears to mean simply sending out directives, and is fundamentally different from mine.
In fact you know what I think of consultation, Madam Speaker. I had a perfect example of consultation during my first experience in following a bill through committee. This was the competition bill and it was designed to change the rules for the corporate sector of this country, outlawing things like double-ticketing, price fixing, pyramid selling and the whole lot. What the government wanted to do was consult first of all with the corporate sector. It spent four years in consultation. It had corporations come before the standing committee to present briefs, and some of the wealthy representatives even had dinner with some members of the committee. These people had their lobby in the other place and they recognized how

June 12, 1975
Indian Affairs
to change the rules. There was no sending out of a directive or bringing in a bill without consultation with that corporate sector.
That is not the kind of consultation which has been carried on with the bands. This consultation has been a kind of one-way consultation. We are talking about two worlds; the world of power, and the government knows how to handle that world of power, and the world of those without power, and the government sure knows how to handle them. There is a big difference in the way the government handles the two, and it better start changing its method because the day is coming.
In fact what the minister calls "consultation" was asking the native peoples to submit briefs to the Contributions to Bands Task Force which was set up in 1972. The native people were asked to submit briefs to this task force which was to study the Grants to Bands Program. In all, 13 briefs were received from native groups across the country.
In April, 1973, the task force took these briefs and produced a draft resolution for discussion purposes. However, this discussion appears to have occured only among officials of Indian affairs, and certainly did not include any representatives of the native people. There was certainly agreement among the Indians that the rules under which funds were made available to bands needed to be clarified and that more efficient means for accounting and auditing were important for the economic and social wellbeing of band members.
Between April, 1973, and February, 1975, when the circulars were first distributed there was no real consultation on how the recommendations would be translated into actual guidelines.
It is not good enough for the minister to say, as he did on May 21, that "we feel that the guidelines respond in many ways to the requests of the native people". His role is not to respond to the native people as though they were children. Even my colleagues on the right have figured out that this is paternalism. It was the Indian affairs branch which drafted the guidelines, that took the recommendations and made them nearly unrecognizable, and that decided they would be promulgated without any discussions with the Indian people.
I would ask the minister now to table all documents and letters his department received which give evidence that the Indian people were consulted on the form and the actual wording of the guidelines he circulated in February of this year. I further ask him to table all documents and letters from native peoples, associations, and band councils which he received subsequent to this date!
Let us be quite clear on what is at stake here today; it is not merely a dispute over whether or not the Indian people were consulted about these circulars. What is at issue here is the credibility of the minister and his department, and his minions therein.
On June 2 the department of Indian affairs issued a communique entitled "Information Summary of Local Government Guidelines for Band Councils and Innuit Settlements". This communique claims first that the "five guidelines are limited to the structure and funding of local government". This surely raises the question of the func-

tion of the band councils which are elected by the members of the band. Despite the term "government", the local government authorities are not elected, and are not responsible to the band members. In fact they are merely extensions of Indian affairs bureaucracy. They exist at the pleasure of the regional director. The regional director may, after consultation with the council, withhold or withdraw the privilege of administering the community program, programs, or parts thereof by the council for whatever length of time deemed necessary.
Such a council, despite the similarity with the term "band council", as defined in the Indian Act, is not accountable to the band itself but only to the Indian affairs bureaucrat. Raising the problem of the band councils' legal ability to assume the powers described in the circulars is merely a ruse to cover up what the department is really trying to do, that is, maintain the Indian people as their personal fiefdom. At the very time the Indian people are developing local and provincial institutions to come to terms with their own problems, Indian Affairs decides to redefine fundamentally the institutions that will decide how band funds are to be spent.
Second, the communique claims that the policy guidelines merely provide for minimal but essential accounting and auditing requirements, delineate responsibilities and, generally speaking, describe the parameters of departmental funding for the many programs involved. Consider, however, what a chartered accountant has to say after reviewing these guidelines. This is what one has to say:
The accounting procedures require an elaborate accounting system. With the exception of very large corporations and other organizations, these requirements are not normally reasonable to expect and are not necessary for an adequate accounting system.
Not only have the minister and his department approached their responsibilities in a paternalistic manner, but they appear also to be incompetent even to carry out the technical aspects of a grants program.
Third, the communique points to the minister's view that the guidelines are of an interim nature. But this is clearly not good enough. On April 1, 1976, Indian Affairs humbly accorded the Indians a chance to take part in a review of the guidelines. After the way these guidelines are being forced on the Indians-that is, in an atmosphere where Indian Affairs officials have threatened to cut off band funds unless the guidelines are accepted-does the Minister really think that Indians can take such promises seriously? His view of consulting is to send out Indian Affairs public relations men to convince the Indians of the department's good intentions two months after he unilaterally issued these guidelines. I do not believe the minister is this naive.
Perhaps the most objectionable part of this public relations blurb from Indian Affairs is that it assumes the Indians are stupid. After telling the native people who, we must remember, have been dealing with an Indian administration system for a hundred years, that their fears are silly, the paper alleges that the guidelines would not really change the present system of chiefs and band councils. The directive, the communique states, made very clear that the chief and council are responsible for plan-
June 12, 1975

ning, estimating, and negotiating for the total needs of the community. Now what is there to worry about? All Indian Affairs is concerned about is protecting Indian culture and helping Indians develop their settlements. But the Indian people are wise; they can read the fine print of the directives like anyone else.
D-l contains the following new definitions for the words chief and council, new in the sense that they go beyond the scope of the Indian Act. According to the directive "chief" means the chief or a band of Indians as defined in the Indian Act, or for the purposes of the circular, the chairman of an Innuit settlement council, and the chairman of a local government authority. The term council also takes on a new meaning. "Council" means the governing body of a band as defined in the Indian Act for the purposes of the circular, or the governing body of a local government authority. I ask hon. members of this House whether, in light of the statement in the communique, this was not a rather obvious attempt at deceit on the part of Indian Affairs?
The entire communique has a patronizing tone to it, "Listen my poor dumb Indians, we mean you no harm." It is clear that the aim of Indian Affairs in its attempts to force these circulars on the native peoples, in its attempts to confuse the issue by using familiar terms such as "chief", "council" and "Government" to cover new institutions, and the minister's strange view of consultation, was to destroy the effectiveness of band councils.
Unlike the local government authorities, the band councils are democratically elected bodies. To deprive the band councils of power over the expenditure of band funds that originate from the department is to deprive them of political power, as Indian Affairs well knows. Yet this is the purpose and intent of these guidelines. They are a blatant attempt to destroy the Indian leadership, a leadership which has the support of their people, and a leadership which has been critical of Indian Affairs personnel. And why shouldn't they be when 42 per cent of a budget of $435 million goes to wages and salaries and for professional and special services, whereas only 31 per cent goes into grants, contributions and other transfer payments to bands?
Will band councils control how band funds are spent, or will this be determined by the new creatures of Indian Affairs? In other words, will Indian Affairs be allowed to continue its colonial domination of the Indian people? The circulars state quite clearly that these "local government authorities" are to be in control of community programs that are "financed in whole or in part by or from department grants, contributions or subsidies." In other words, controlled not by a band's elected officials but by Indian Affairs.
I find it strange that a government which claims to understand the nature of colonialism in the Third World and which wishes to protect Canadians from American cultural imperialism in the form of Reader's Digest and Time magazine cannot understand that it itself has a long history of being a colonial master to the Indians. The Minority Rights Group suggests that this is because of a lack of humility. In my experience such an explanation does not suffice. In any colonial situation someone always benefits from colonialism. In this case we know it is not the Indians. Who does the minister think benefits?
Indian Affairs
In conclusion I just want to say I listened to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) not so long ago talk about the moral responsibility we as Canadians have to the Third World countries in ensuring that they have proper energy devices such as the CANDU reactor. I and he recognize this moral responsibility, but I want to ask whether the government recognizes its moral responsibility to the Indian people of Canada. I have visited the Yukon Territory. There are no reserves there. There is no reason why the government should not solve the problems there. The problems in respect of housing there are pitiable, but the government sits on its hands and does nothing.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I suppose I might consider myself a veteran in this House of Commons in the sense that I have been here seven years and there are not now in the House too many members from British Columbia who were here at the time I was first elected. I want to say that during the years I have been here as a member of parliament I have heard much rhetoric.
I think if we were to read today's debate and all the rhetoric put forward we would find many duplications in the speeches made on both sides of the House. I think this rhetoric, this feeling, or whatever one might call it, is a very sincere effort on the part of all members of parliament. This is good.
I can remember not too long ago that it was not very often when matters pertaining to Indian Affairs came before the House of Commons. That was bad. So even though I think many of the things said here today can perhaps be categorized as rhetoric, nevertheless it is very important because I am aware of the sincerity and desire of hon. members on all sides of the House to do the right thing for the Indian people. But we have a long way to go.
One of the things that I was thinking about when some hon. members were speaking was that the hon. member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth) and myself should wonder to ourselves what kind of country we would have, or whether in fact this debate would be necessary tonight, if our ancestors had had a different immigration policy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REQUEST GOVERNMENT UNDERTAKE FULL CONSULTATION WITH NATIVE PEOPLE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING POLICY
speechtext:
It is important that we look at the situation of the Indian people, that we look at where the Indian people are going. It is important that the Indian people be involved and that they set the objectives that they want for themselves. This is the kind of message that is coming from the debate tonight and from the whole process of consultation.
There is much talk about consultation, and that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Buchanan) did not consult enough, did not do this and that. I want to reach a point somewhere along the line, way down the road, when we will not have to count Indians all the time and we will not always have to count women. Instead of counting Indians and saying how wrong the minister was, and how wrong everybody else

June 12, 1975
Indian Affairs
was, the Indian people must arrive at some point of total independence within their own communities; they must find themselves and live the kind of life they want to live as individuals. This is the kind of future for which the Indian people should strive.
I want to deal for a few moments with some of the things that were said by the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle). I know that hon. members can get carried away with some of the things they say. He said that the minister appears to undermine the organizations and district councils by giving so much authority to band councils. I hope he was not serious when he said that, and I hope he did not really mean it. It is a gross error on his part because in developing autonomy, Indian organizations such a district councils, and indeed the National Indian Brotherhood and the Union of British Columbia Indian Chiefs, must get their authority from the band councils. Band councils are the individual administrative units so far as the administration of Indian affairs in this country is concerned. So I hope the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River, who is a very sincere member with regard to the native people in this country, will reconsider what he said.
A number of hon. members, such as the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson), the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River and perhaps others, have mentioned that the Union of B.C. Chiefs made some pretty important decisions a few weeks ago in that province. At a time of absolute frustration about the conditions in which they found themselves and about some of the things that have not been done, they rejected outright any further services of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
In the time that I have been associated with Indian organizations I have never seen such a fundamental decision made by any organization. This is not just a bunch of radicals who have made this decision, nor is it an empty gesture on their part which they may later reconsider. This is a real, honest, sincere, fundamental re-examination which is going on in the reserve communities of British Columbia, a fundamental re-assessment such as I have never seen before.
I have urged the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to respond to this call from the Indians of B.C. in the most positive manner possible, and I am glad that he has taken much of my advice. He made a very important statement on May 30, which appeared in a press release, regarding the future of Indian affairs in that province. The first paragraph reads:
Indian affairs minister, Judd Buchanan, stated that he would welcome discussions with British Columbia Indians in response to their call for the transfer to them of more responsibility for the running of their own affairs.
That is great. I am glad that this is going on, and I am glad of the re-examination that is going on in Kamloops, Vernon, and in many other parts of British Columbia. So far as Kamloops and Vernon are concerned, for instance, the minister said that he is willing to close the offices there. Discussions are now going on between the regional director in the province of British Columbia and a number of Indian bands in the area that I represent.

The kind of questions that the Indian people there are asking themselves are: where are we going? Will we be forever dependent upon the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the great white father in Ottawa, or should we try to change the kind of life that we want for our people? Will we try to give them a meaningful, independent way of life? This is the kind of fundamental examination that is going on. This is why I told the minister that some of the voices that are heard from out there might sound a little angry. But they are angry for a lot of good reasons.
The Indians of British Columbia, and indeed Indians all across Canada, including non-status Indians, have a lot of things to be angry about, and that is what they are saying in British Columbia. This is not just a frivolous attitude they are adopting toward these questions. There is a fundamental re-examination going on, and the minister, and indeed parliament, must respond to these voices which now sound angry. Even though much of the discussion in British Columbia has centred around programs and around administration, behind it all there is a much deeper problem facing them, namely, the whole question about aboriginal rights, land settlement, treaty rights, and fishing and hunting rights. This is at the top of their list. This is the big reason why they are angry.
The Indians of British Columbia-and we can include Indians in other areas-have not had a good deal in so far as the settlement of their rights is concerned. They have had a poor land deal. For instance, the Indians of Alberta receive under their treaty about 1.6 million acres of land, and there are a little over 30,000 Indians in Alberta now. That is a rough figure to give some kind of illustration. The Indians of British Columbia have around 700,000 acres, in round figures, and yet the Indian population in British Columbia numbers over 50,000. That is an illustration of the kind of bad deal which the Indian people in British Columbia got.
Some other situations arose where certain bands were given land, and then a commission came along and said that some of these reserves were too big. I doubt that very much. But deciding that these reserves were too big, they cut them down. And so 36,000 acres of reserve land in British Columbia were cut off. This is another very serious grievance.
I know that in some instances the Indians realize that there are cities built on what used to be Indian land, for example, the city of Penticton. Indians realize they will not get these cities back. Some of my friends say, "As I look across the river I see that the white man has built cement basements. I think he is going to stay here for a while." They know that in towns like Vernon, my old home area, there were several acres cut off. These people realize they will not get that land back, but they want some redress for the injustices imposed upon them when these lands were taken away. In addition to the land, they want redress for the hunting rights and fishing rights, something which they did not receive on an equivalent basis to many other provinces across the country.
I would just like to close by endorsing some of the comments made by hon. colleague from Comox-Alberni
June 12, 1975

about the settlement of the land question in British Columbia, or the settlement of aboriginal rights in the province of British Columbia. Much has been said over the years. There have been many joint committee studies, many reports and so on. The former leader of the NDP in the province of British Columbia, who is now Mr. Justice Berger, for whom I have the highest regard, went so far as to take the Nishga claims against the British Columbia government to the Supreme Court of Canada. I wish a few more members of the NDP were here tonight so that I could ask them to review the position which was taken by Mr. Justice Berger.
