subtopic: PENITENTIARIES-BRITISH COLUMBIA-RESPONSIBILITY FOR RELEASE OF DRUGS TO PRISONERS AND HOSTAGES AND FOR INFORMING HOSTAGES GUARDS WOULD MOVE WHEN HOSTAGES MOVED AGAINST PRISONERS
PENITENTIARIES-BRITISH COLUMBIA-RESPONSIBILITY FOR RELEASE OF DRUGS TO PRISONERS AND HOSTAGES AND FOR INFORMING HOSTAGES GUARDS WOULD MOVE WHEN HOSTAGES MOVED AGAINST PRISONERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise in the adjournment debate with regard to some questions I asked yesterday and today regarding the sad tragedy in the British Columbia penitentiary where three inmates took 15 hostages and put the proposition to the government that they be allowed to take a helicopter to Vancouver International Airport, and from there to take an airplane to a country which would accept them.
We heard many answers yesterday from the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand), and today from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) because the Solicitor General had to be absent from the House, but there are still many questions to be answered on this subject. From the government all we will have will be an internal inquiry, and my party has been asking for a public inquiry, a judicial inquiry, by one of the supreme court justices of this country. We feel that the Canadian people must be given many answers which will explain the tragedy to them.
The minister said that the government tried to make a deal with foreign countries, which was unsuccessful, but that one country agreed to accept these three men, on condition that when these men landed they would be incarcerated and immediately returned to Canada. We have also heard the story of one of the hostages who says that he was told, by one of the hostages who had made a telephone call-the inmates allowed the hostages to telephone their loved ones-that the penitentiary officials were ready for action by the hostages against the prisoners who were holding them. As soon as they were to take action, the penitentiary officials would be ready to assist and attack. This gave those who had been the hostages of the inmates for a number of hours the idea that they would have to do something.
We are then told by one of the hostages that between 11 and 11.30 one of the intermediaries visited them and gave them the same story he had given them a number of times, that the government was still working on the case and that it might be able to get a country to accept the prisoners. Yet, according to what was said in this House, the government knew at least three hours before this that one country would take the inmates. The hostages took this message from the intermediary to mean that they would have to attack, and they planned their attack from that point forward.
We have also heard from the hostages that the inmates were provided with a drug called noludar. The inmates forced the hostages to take the drug, which virtually
[The Acting Speaker (Mrs. Morin).]
rendered them helpless. The drug company which supplies this drug advises me that one ounce, or 28.1 millilitres, is the normal daily dose for an adult. The hostage told me that the hostages were forced to take up to seven ounces of this drug, which immobilized them on the first night.
On the second night, after a message had been passed by somebody in the penitentiary system to the hostages, and after the statement had been made by the intermediaries, the hostages were afraid that if they had to take the drug again they might never wake up. Madam Speaker, these people were in a very difficult situation.
What happened also puts the government in a difficult position. It explained to this House that these people, the hostages, had an idea as to what was happening but, according to our information, we know they did not. They attacked and, as everybody knows, a lady lost her life.
The discrepancies between the hostages' story and what the government said happened are so great that we suggest the matter can only be resolved if the government appoints a supreme court justice to head a public inquiry immediately.
This evening something was broadcast on the Vancouver radio station which made me sick to my stomach. I learned that one of the ladies who was still in the room with the 14 hostages-the lady who was killed was in another room with two of the other inmates-took drugs voluntarily, I am told, because she was so afraid for her own life. Madam Speaker, when the guards burst into that room, this lady was having sexual intercourse with one of the inmates. I think it is sad that this had to go that far, that this person was so afraid for her life that she had to take that action. Because nothing was happening, she was forced to go that far.
I will end by pleading with the government to do something. We are raising this matter on a non-partisan basis; we do not want to turn this into a political issue, because we know that conditions in penitentiaries are so bad that no prison units exit in this country which can cope with them. Many problems are involved in this issue, and my party will be quite prepared not to comment on them, if only we knew that a capable judge in this country will be appointed to look into this issue on a non-partisan basis, and tell the people of Canada not only what happened in this tragedy but how to solve this problem, so that this sort of thing will never again happen.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gilles Marceau (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PENITENTIARIES-BRITISH COLUMBIA-RESPONSIBILITY FOR RELEASE OF DRUGS TO PRISONERS AND HOSTAGES AND FOR INFORMING HOSTAGES GUARDS WOULD MOVE WHEN HOSTAGES MOVED AGAINST PRISONERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like in the first place to apologize for the absence of the Minister and say that due to his illness which is a minor one but very painful, he is not here this evening. I can say that I happened to be with the minister at a party Sunday evening in Toronto when he became suddenly ill, before to the events in question.
My hon. friend asked two questions. He will understand that in the short period which has elapsed since those events, it was impossible to obtain a full answer because, of course, several persons needed rest after it was all over.
In reply to the first question, I should like to reassure my colleague by telling him that the authorities did not give any instruction to the hostages and that the later did

not notify the authorities of their intention to attack the inmates. The orders at first were that an assault was allowed only in case of serious trouble inside. Now, nothing of the kind happened, and it is the hostages themselves who made the decision without receiving any orders nor notifying the authorities.
As far as drugs are concerned, I must say to my hon. friend that drugs had been prescribed by the doctor of the institution. Drugs were given to the inmates and in only one case to a hostage. Drugs were not given to the inmates to be given to the hostages, but it may have happened that the inmates asked the hostages to take the drugs because they suspected poisoning.
Therefore, I must say that the drugs in question were innocuous. They were anti-psychotic drugs, tranquillizers or hypnotics, and Noludar is a hypnotic. I agree that there is nothing political about this matter and I can assure my colleague that I shall convey his views to the Solicitor General. I think that the matter should be aired and I hope the opposition will co-operate with the government in its investigation, and especially to see to it that such tragic events never happen again.

subtopic: HOUSING-REQUEST TOP PRIORITY BE GIVEN PROJECT IN CAPE BRETON COUNTY
HOUSING-REQUEST TOP PRIORITY BE GIVEN PROJECT IN CAPE BRETON COUNTY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, sometimes in this House, and in this city which reeks of economic security with well-off government workers, there seems to be an air of unreality. It seems to be difficult in this environment for even ministers of the Crown to grasp that there are many, many Canadians who are ill fed and ill housed.
I represent in this House of Commons a people, many of whom are ill housed to such a degree that the new regional manager of Central Mortgage and Housing operating out of Halifax says the housing situation is one of the worst in Nova Scotia and, indeed, in Canada.
Yet that same institution, Central Mortgage and Housing, received an application on December 14, 1972, asking that 80 family units be constructed in the Dinn Street area of Glace Bay. Despite the unbelievable need, it was not until February 8, 1975, that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation announced that a beginning was to be made on the construction of these houses.
Would you believe, Madam Speaker, that the cooperation and coordination have been so bad in Nova Scotia that, despite the desperate need in Cape Breton County, hundreds of thousands of dollars of federal funds for housing were unused by the Nova Scotia Housing Commission last year? There is also an element of unreality in Halifax government circles with their insistence that there is no need of public housing any more in Nova Scotia. This attitude, among other things, has held up the signing of an agreement between the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the Nova Scotia Housing Commission. We know who gets shortchanged in these bureaucratic snafus.
In the area of Glace Bay, 200 of the applicants for housing are making under $4,500. That is right, Madam Speaker, under $4,500!
Adjournment Debate
The Cape Breton Development Corporation recently entered into the home construction field in co-operation with a private firm. I believe that eventually this will be a real contribution to decent housing for our people.
On this occasion I make a special appeal to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) to take the lead in bringing together CMHC's Regional Director for Nova Scotia, the experts on the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program and on Rural and Native Housing, the Regional Representative of the Nova Scotia Housing Commission in Sydney, along with Mr. David Miller the VicePresident of Development for DEVCO, to discuss the possibilities of coming up with a permanent rehabilitation program to deal with much of the housing stock in the mining and rural areas of Cape Breton since there is no way, other than rehabilitation, to answer the need. The programs of rehabilitation presently going on are done on a sort of hit and run basis depending upon impermanent and uncertain LIP grants and special small allotments from CMHC regional funds.
The Pensioners' Union of Cape Breton, and the Cape Breton Labour Council as well as other prominent voluntary housing organizations in the area would be most anxious to assist-if it is thought feasible-with any aspect of such a permanent rehabilitation program carried out under the direction of the Cape Breton Development Corporation which happily, as noted previously, has already broken new ground recently by taking an equity position in setting up a new housing construction company designed to build new homes in the area at a price not exceeding $20,000.
The rehabilitation program would, of course also provide badly needed jobs in an area in which the actual number of unemployed-I am using unemployment insurance figures-was 9,115 last winter in Cape Breton County, and which, in labour force survey terms, for Cape Breton Island saw 13 per cent of the labour force unemployed in January, 16.1 per cent in February, 17 per cent in March, and 14.3 per cent in April, the last official figures available. This averages 7 to 8 per cent higher than group six of the economic region of Nova Scotia which includes the County of Halifax.
It should be obvious to the Minister for Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) that long term development efforts by the Cape Breton Development Corporation are not sufficient to meet the ongoing unemployment and underemployment problems in that area. I was keenly disappointed in the vague and unassuring answer he gave me yesterday. Surely special efforts at solving this housing crisis would at the same time cut down expenditures on unemployment insurance and other transfer payments that are necessary even just to keep many of the unemployed and underemployed in that region going on a bare existence basis.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gilles Marceau (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: HOUSING-REQUEST TOP PRIORITY BE GIVEN PROJECT IN CAPE BRETON COUNTY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Barnett Danson), I am pleased to reply to the remarks of the hon. member on housing in Cape Breton.

June 12, 1975
Adjournment Debate

As the minister stated in the House on June 11, he has met with the provincial housing minister both in Halifax and in Ottawa in recent days, and they are in agreement that housing conditions in Cape Breton deserve a high priority in terms of federal and provincial funds. I would point out that in 1974 almost exactly one third of the funds committed under the Housing Act in Nova Scotia were committed in Cape Breton-more than $20 million.
The City of Sydney was selected as one of the three in Nova Scotia for assistance through the Neighbourhood Improvement Program under the 1974 agreement. Our latest information is that the provincial minister is expected to sign the 1975 Neighbourhood Improvement Program agreement today. The selection of centres to receive assistance under the 1975 agreement will proceed after the signing, and the province will soon be requesting CMHC's concurrence in these selections. Also, the cities concerned will be designating specific neighbourhoods in which program funds are to be spent.
Negotiations between CMHC and the Nova Scotia Housing Commission with respect to the rural and native housing program under section 40 of the National Housing Act have been completed, and the agreement is to be signed on June 23.
Upon the completion of the above agreements the NHA programs for rural and native housing, residential rehabilitation assistance, assisted home ownership, public housing and emergency repair will all be applied in Cape Breton. Selection or designation of the most deserving areas will follow as quickly as possible.
With reference specifically to Glace Bay, the project of 80 family units mentioned in the Halifax press, this was committed in December 1973, not 1972, and the start was delayed while land was being serviced by the town in co-operation with the Nova Scotia Housing Commission. I might add that a project of 40 senior citizen units has been committed for Glace Bay and is currently at the design stage.
Since May 26 the construction on the 80 unit project has been held up by a strike, as is the case with 60 unit senior citizen project in Sydney and a 60 unit senior citizen project in Cape Breton county.

I can assure my friend that I shall refer the recommendations he made tonight to the minister and ask him to take them into consideration.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-SUGGESTED INCREASE IN RESEARCH GRANTS TO UNIVERSITIES AND STUDY OF DUPLICATION
AGRICULTURE-SUGGESTED INCREASE IN RESEARCH GRANTS TO UNIVERSITIES AND STUDY OF DUPLICATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, last week I asked the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) a question having to do with the allocation of funds for research by the Department of Agriculture to the many universities we have in this great country of Canada. I feel we are missing an unique opportunity better to co-ordinate our funds to universities in order not to duplicate facilities and buildings being constructed by the government.

In no way do I wish to take away from the tremendous performance of the Department of Agriculture research branch. We have a good record, and when we compare it with that of other countries we realize that the budget that the Department of Agriculture provides to universities is among the best in the world. But I am concerned that even with this record we could do a better job.
In the budget for this year there is an item of $850,000 in the estimates of the Department of Agriculture for grants to universities. The budget is approximately $85 million. In other words, one per cent is going toward research at universities. This one per cent has been constant over the past years. The problem is that the research capabilities of the universities are stifled because the grants given to them are generally for one or two years, and the money is insufficient to enable them to continue projects beyond a very short period of time.
It would make much more sense to me if there were better co-ordination between the Department of Agriculture, the universities and research professors regarding money spent on facilities that require to be built to embrace new scopes in the research field, as well as buildings being constructed by the department on their research stations. Certainly if we could co-ordinate the use of these buildings so that not only research people but students could use them, we would be in a better position to train new agricultural students who would be capable of entering into agricultural research areas the better to provide the farmers and others in agriculture with the necessary techniques to meet their needs.
The problem I see now is that the capabilities of a university professor who has time to work in research are limited because he is provided with an insufficient amount of money to hire technicians or students in the summer to work on projects. One university professor with a doctorate degree could look after and co-ordinate the efforts of 10 or 12 technicians working in different fields in an attempt to come up with perhaps a new variety of crop within a certain period of time. Such a professor requires a definite budget to hire those people so he will know he can start and finish his project.
When you try to spread $850,000 among 30, 40 or 50 universities it does not go very far. We presently have 38 research stations dividing $85 million or $90 million. With that type of a budget you can do something.
The whole point of my question is an attempt to persuade the minister in the future to try to co-ordinate better the use of this $90 million by the universities and research departments so that we can perhaps do an even better job than we are now doing.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joseph-Philippe Guay (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-SUGGESTED INCREASE IN RESEARCH GRANTS TO UNIVERSITIES AND STUDY OF DUPLICATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in representing the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) this evening I should like to bring to the attention of the hon. member and the House that in 1963 the total amount of money paid toward education and research as such was $236 million. When the right hon. Lester Pearson was in office he wanted education to be provided Canadians as a right. Since those days the money
June 12, 1975

spent on education has increased annually. For the year 1974-75 in ail forms of grants to universities the amount was in excess of $3 billion. I thought I should put the emphasis on that first. It shows the government's concern in respect of education and research.
Having regard to research, which is really the point of the hon. member's question, I should like to put on the record some figures in respect of the amounts of money and percentages of the GNP for the year 1969. I will give the name of the countries first, then the percentage in respect of universities and then in respect of governments. They are as follows: Canada, .39 for universities and .47 for the government; the USA, .34 for the universities and .40 for the government; the United Kingdom, .18 for universities and .54 for the government; France, .27 for the universities and .56 for the government; Sweden, .25 for universities and .20 for the government; Germany, .30 for universities and .08 for the government; Japan, .30 for universities and .20 for the government, and the Netherlands, .37 for the universities and .24 for the government.
The only research grants the Department of Agriculture is responsible for are those awarded annually as university operating grants, totalling $650,000 per year. The pur-
Adjournment Debate
pose of these grants is primarily to support research by graduate students in agriculture, rather than the general conduct of university agricultural research.
This latter phase of research is largely supported by operating grants from the National Research Council which has several times our amount of money designated for university research support, including agricultural facilities.
At the present time the research granting function of the federal government is being reviewed, and an announcement on future responsibility is expected later this year.
The recent formation of the Canadian Agricultural Research Council hopefully will provide a mechanism for improved co-ordination and interaction of the universities and government and their respective research programs. Good progress is being made and should help alleviate some of the criticism of federal domination in the activities of the Canadian Agricultural Services Co-ordinating Committee which advises the department on agricultural policies. I wish to assure you, Madam Speaker, that the minister told me he is looking into this particular aspect.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.27 p.m.
